case_summary.text: Remand to permit employer evidence unjustified as no domestic enquiry held or reservation made in written statement:HC
HC quashes dismissal of tea estate workmen as domestic enquiries violated natural justice; directs Labour Court to decide merits
Labour Court must allow additional evidence if domestic enquiry is held unfair; remand justified:HC
Finding u/s 33(2)(b) of Industrial Disputes Act on fairness of domestic enquiry is binding and operates as res judicata in later dispute: HC

LABOUR LAWS: Where Management had reserved its right to adduce additional evidence if domestic enquiry was held to be unfair, but Labour Court decided dispute finally based on enquiry officer’s report and evidence already on record without deciding fairness of enquiry as a preliminary issue, opportunity to let in additional evidence stood denied to Management, thereby affecting its right to defend case, and, thus, award was liable to be set aside and matter remanded for fresh consideration

LABOUR LAW : Finding under section 33(2)(b) of Industrial Disputes Act as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper is binding on parties to proceeding as authority has jurisdiction to adjudicate on fairness of domestic enquiry and said finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute assailing order of penalty as it operates as res judicata between same parties in a subsequent proceeding.

LABOUR LAWS : Where workman was not allowed to be defended by a lawyer in domestic enquiry, however, he had in extension cross-examined management witnesses and had also re-examined himself, he was not seriously prejudiced in being denied services of a lawyer in domestic enquiry

LABOUR LAWS: Where Tribunal framed an issue on validity of domestic enquiry but failed to render any finding thereon and proceeded to decide remaining issues on merits, and management had not sought preliminary adjudication of said issue, award directing reinstatement with back wages could not be sustained and matter was liable to be remanded for fresh determination of issues in proper sequence
Failure to decide validity of domestic enquiry vitiated reinstatement award; matter remanded:HC

INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where employer dismissed petitioner solely due to an offence registration without conducting domestic enquiry and failed to reserve right to adduce evidence on misconduct in its written statement, Industrial Court erred in remanding matter for employer to prove misconduct and its order was to be set aside.

LABOUR LAWS: Where Management terminated a workman after a domestic enquiry for serious misconduct and Conciliation Officer approved termination, but Labour Court treated officer’s findings as beyond jurisdiction, Labour Court could not decide correctness of enquiry as though sitting in appeal over such approval, but could allow Management to lead evidence if prima facie prejudice was shown, making Labour Court’s order liable to be set aside

U.P. INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where employee designated as Production Supervisor claimed no supervisory powers and performed only clerical tasks, and employer failed to lead evidence regarding actual duties to rebut his status as a workman, Labour Court rightly found violation of natural justice in domestic enquiry, declared termination illegal, and such findings could not be interfered with under Article 227, warranting dismissal of employer's petition.

LABOUR LAWS: Where charges were framed against petitioner-conductor regarding cash and ticket irregularities, however, without conducting an enquiry, respondent-corporation had passed a final order whereby petitioner's annual increment was withheld for a period of six months, punishment imposed by respondent-corporation was not legally sustainable
Labour Court not barred from exhibiting domestic enquiry evidence under Section 11A; dismissal upheld:HC

INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where workman was dismissed after a fair and proper domestic enquiry and Labour Court merely fixed case for production and marking of documents already part of enquiry record for proper appraisal, such action did not constitute taking fresh evidence and was not barred by proviso to Section 11A, and Labour Court rightly upheld dismissal after appreciating all relevant materials.
Once chance was given to workmen to lodge their claims, no further opportunity of hearing to be given: NCLT

INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where a mob of workers at Tea Estate committed acts of violence leading to dismissal of eleven workmen after domestic enquiries, Labour Court wrongly upheld dismissals without framing a preliminary issue on enquiry validity and failed to consider proportionality of punishment, so matter deserved interference under Article 226 due to violation of principles of natural justice and was remanded for fresh decision on merits based on available evidence.

Competition Act : Where investigations revealed that "Indian Jute Mills Association" & "Gunny Trade Association " ('IJMA') & ('GTA') were engaged in anti-competitive practices and penalty was imposed upon association and its office-bearers and members of Executive Committee, in the absence of a determination by the Commission that appellants had abused their dominant position in the relevant market, CCI could not have imposed penalty upon appellants holding them guilty of anti-competitive
SC : quashes CVC direction that pending a criminal investigation, departmental proceedings are to be held in abeyance
SC : quashes CVC direction that pending a criminal investigation, departmental proceedings are to be held in abeyance
Interference with punishment unwarranted after charges were proved in a fair enquiry; 25% back wages granted considering respondent's age : HC
Suspension and issuance of a charge sheet alter service conditions, giving workman a statutory right to raise an industrial dispute : HC
Closure of industrial unit without compliance of Chapter V-B void as adverse inference drawn from non-production of wage records:HC
Workman reinstatement with proportionate back wages mandated for dismissal during legally pending reference:HC

LABOUR LAW : Where bus driver met with an accident with tractor and disciplinary authority imposed punishment of deferment of bus driver's annual increment for a period of one year with cumulative effect, since police case had been registered against tractor driver, who was facing criminal trial but domestic enquiry officer drew erroneous conclusions and ignored supporting evidence, punishment was found to be shockingly disproportionate thus, Labour Court rightly set aside punishment order
Delay in inquiry beyond timeline under CCS (CCA) Rules does not vitiate proceedings without prejudice shown: HC

INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES ACT: Where petitioner textile company failed to comply with prescribed procedure for closure application under Rule 82-B and sought to invoke deeming provision for retrospective closure under Section 25-O(3), such claim was not allowed as application was incomplete and decided within statutory period, making petitioner ineligible for relief under deeming provision but permitted to seek review or adjudication under Section 25-O(5), hence writ petition was dismissed.
Onus on union to prove employees are 'workmen' under S.2(s) of ID Act for complaint maintainability:SC

LABOUR LAWS: Where employee alleged oral termination without notice and non-compliance with mandatory provisions of Industrial Disputes Act, and Labour Court recorded absence of notice, domestic enquiry, and unchallenged evidence while petitioners-employer failed to offer convincing explanation for delay, there was no good reason to unsettle concurrent orders and interference was unwarranted, leading to dismissal of writ petition

COMPETITION LAW : Where CCI held that OP-MMBL held a dominant position in relevant market of provision of Bt. Cotton Technology in India as well as downstream market of manufacture and sale of Bt. Cotton seeds in India and ordered investigation against OP for charging excessive and unfair prices for Bt. Technology,

LABOUR LAWS : Where a bank employee was discharged from service after a fair domestic enquiry in which charges were proved, Tribunal's interference in punishment was unwarranted, though considering respondent's age and long unemployment, award was modified to entitle him only to 25% back wages from discharge date till superannuation without interest
Matter remanded as Labour Court passed award without hearing arguments on behalf of workmen: HC

LABOUR LAWS: Where proceedings were initiated under Factories Act and IPC for same factory accident, petition to quash proceedings under Factories Act on ground of double jeopardy was not maintainable, as Factories Act, being a special enactment, prevailed and disputed facts were matters for trial
Dismissal of workman is invalid and liable to be quashed as disciplinary authority failed to consider his reply: HC
CL: At first motion stage in an application under section 391 workmen have no right to be heard

LABOUR LAWS : Where disciplinary proceedings were pending against five out of seven workmen proposed for recognition as protected workmen, management was well within its right to decline recognition to such workmen and, therefore, order passed by Assistant Labour Commissioner declaring all seven workmen as protected workmen was to be set aside
AA couldn't decide disputed fact as to whether workmen had actually worked during CIRP: NCLAT
Corporation can invoke Section 45A only if employer fails to produce records or obstructs inspection : SC
CCI directs probe against 'Mahyco Monsanto' for imposing stringent terms on sub-licensing of Bt. Cotton technology
Written demand isn’t needed for conciliation; govt can refer disputes to Labour Court to prevent unrest : SC
Quash petition against Factories Act prosecution on ground of double jeopardy dismissed: HC
Labour Court can't review approval order u/s 33(2)(b) of Industrial Disputes Act as an appellate authority; may permit evidence if enquiry caused prejudice: HC

LABOUR LAWS: Where misconduct against a conductor was not proved due to non-verification of cash, inconsistent passenger statements and a vitiated enquiry, reinstatement with continuity of service and consequential benefits, though without back wages, was justified

■

By Award dated 29.02.2016 in Reference Case No. 02/2009, the Labour Court upheld the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld the dismissal of the workmen; no separate finding on proportionality of the punishment was recorded.

■

On writ petition to the High Court.

HELD: ■ The narration of facts herein above and a perusal of the impugned Award would show that the learned Labour Court did not specifically frame a preliminary issue as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries which were held against the workmen. It is apposite out here to mention that at paragraph Nos. 5, 6, and 7 as well as at paragraph No. 14 of the written statement filed by the management, the reports of the domestic enquiries were relied upon by the management to justify their stand for dismissing the workmen. Under such circumstances, it was the requirement of law that the learned Labour Court ought to have framed a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries held against the workmen. [Para 22]

■

This Court also finds it pertinent to observe that a perusal of the impugned Award shows that though no preliminary issue was framed regarding the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports, but what was decided in the impugned Award was only the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports. The learned Labour Court further did not proceed to decide anything else. [Para 23]

■

It surprises this Court to take note of that the learned Labour Court while passing the impugned Award, after upholding the domestic enquiries held against the workmen, did not decide as regards the proportionality of the punishments which have been imposed against the workmen, which was a jurisdiction conferred upon the learned Labour Court to decide. The procedure therefore followed by the learned Labour Court, in the opinion of this Court amounts to a jurisdictional error committed by the learned Labour Court. [Para 24]

■

This Court finds it very pertinent to take note of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of M.L. Singla v. Punjab National Bank [2019] 9 taxmann.com 1153 (SC)/(2018) 18 SCC 21, wherein the Supreme Court observed the procedure to be followed when a domestic enquiry is being relied upon. [Para 25]

■

The proposition of law as laid down by the Supreme Court in M.L. Singla (supra) clearly show that when a domestic enquiry is being relied upon, it is the requirement of law that the preliminary issue be framed as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry report and thereupon, if it is held that the domestic enquiry report is in order, then to decide as to whether the imposition of punishment was proportionate. In the instant case, it would be seen that the learned Labour Court vide the impugned Award only decided as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports and held it to be fair and thereupon upheld the termination of the workmen. [Para 26]

■

Taking into account the submissions so made by the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, this Court finds it pertinent to look into, as to whether, the opinion rendered by the learned Labour Court holding the domestic enquiries to be fair is in consonance with the well-settled principles of law. [Para 27]

■

From a perusal of the materials on record, and more particularly, the evidence adduced by the management witness No.4 before the learned Labour Court, who was the Enquiry Officer, he during his cross-examination, categorically mentioned that though information was provided to the workmen as regards the appointment of an Enquiry Officer and to participate in the domestic enquiry proceedings, but he did not inform the workmen that they are required to adduce evidence. In fact, during his cross-examination, he mentioned that the Presenting Officer would be informing the workmen that they would be required to adduce evidence. [Para 28]

■

This Court also finds it very surprising to take note of that without the records of the domestic enquiries being placed before the learned Labour Court as to how the evidence was adduced and as to whether the observers were present inasmuch as such evidence would be available in the Minutes recorded during the course of the domestic enquiries. [Para 29]

■

10. This Court does not propose to examine the said issue in this petition. [Para 11]

■

The petitioner's contention that criminal prosecution cannot be initiated under Section 34 pending adjudication of the dispute under Section 10, where the allegations in both proceedings are one and the same cannot be accepted in absolute terms. In appropriate cases, there can be simultaneous proceedings under Sections 10 and 34. In some cases, the simultaneous proceedings may not be desirable. [Para 13] ■

While considering such a question on permissibility of simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication proceeding, in the context of two different enactments, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO ([1984] 19 Taxman 1 (SC) /1984 (Supp) SCC 437), and Radheshyam Kejriwal v. State of West Bengal ([2011] 12 taxmann.com 107/108 SCL 406 (SC)/(2011) 3 SCC 581) has held that such criminal prosecution pending adjudication of dispute is permissible. On behalf of the respondent-Union, these two judgments are cited to justify the simultaneous application under Sections 10 and 34. [Para 14]

■

In P. Jayappan (supra), the Apex Court was considering Section 276-C of Income Tax Act, 1961 (Act, 1961) and in Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), Section 56 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (Act, 1973). In both the enactments, the provisions of law provide for simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of a claim or liability under the said Acts. [Para 15]

■

Section 276-C of Act, 1961 which provides for criminal prosecution, uses the expression "without prejudice to any penalty that may be imposable on him under any other provisions of this Act". Likewise, Section 56 of the Act, 1973, uses the expression "Without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under this Act". [Para 16]

■

From the language employed in the aforementioned two provisions, it is explicit that, the simultaneous criminal prosecution for the violation of the provisions of the aforementioned two Acts, even before the adjudication takes place on the claim or liability under the respective Acts, is expressly provided. [Para 17]

■

In the Act there is no provision which uses similar expression which expressly provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution and adjudication of a claim or liability under the Act. Thus, in a way it is possible to urge a contention that, the simultaneous prosecution pending adjudication of the dispute alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is not permissible. [Para 18]

■

At the same time, one has to notice that there is no provision which specifically bars simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of any claim or liability by any other authority/Tribunal/Court under the Act. [Para 19]

■

To answer the questions raised, the Court has to keep in mind the object of the Act. One of the objects is to provide efficacious remedy to the workmen against the violations of the provisions of the Act. At the same time, among other, the Act also aims in securing industrial peace. [Para 20]

■

If these two aspects are borne in mind, it is not permissible to accept the contention that the complaint under Section 34 alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is permissible only in a situation where the adjudication gets concluded by the authority/Court/Tribunal relating to the violation of the provisions of the Act. [Para 21]

■

At the same time it is not possible to accept the contention that every application alleging violation of the provisions of the Act, seeking permission to prosecute for alleged violation of the provisions of the Act, will have to be allowed pending adjudication of the dispute arising from such violations of the provisions of the Act. [Para 22]

■

Both contentions referred to above are extreme contentions and such an interpretation also does not augur well with the object and purpose of Section 34. [Para 23]

■

At this juncture, it is relevant to notice the ratio in Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), where the Act, 1973 expressly provided simultaneous prosecution. Paragraph No.38 of the said judgment reads as under: " (vi) The finding in the adjudication proceedings in favour of the person facing trial for identical violation will depend upon the nature of finding. If the exoneration in adjudication proceedings is on technical ground and not on merit, prosecution may continue; and (vii) In case of exoneration, however, on merits where the allegation is found to be not sustainable at all and the person held innocent, criminal prosecution on the same set of facts and circumstances cannot be allowed to continue, the underlying principle being the higher standard of proof in criminal cases. " [Para 24]

■

The ratio is laid down in the context of Act, 1973. Section 56 of said Act, 1973 which provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution and uses the expression "without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under the Act.'" [Para 25]

■

The interpretation that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited cannot be stretched to contend that the finding as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper is not on adjudication. For the reasons recorded above, it is held that the finding on the issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory. And said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging the penalty. [Para 35]

■ In the case on hand, the Court has secured the records pertaining to the proceeding under section 33(2)(b) and after going through the said records, it is noticed that the parties have led evidence on the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. Later, the finding is recorded holding that the enquiry was fair and proper, and approval is granted for dismissal of the employee. [Para 36]

■

Conclusions: (a) The enquiry under section 33(2)(b), as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper, is adjudicatory. (b) The enquiry under section 33(2)(b) as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper (rendered after recording of evidence before the authority) is binding on the parties to the proceeding as the authority has the jurisdiction to adjudicate on the fairness of the domestic enquiry and said finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute assailing the order of penalty as it operates as Res judicata between the same parties in a subsequent proceeding. (c) The Authority under section 33(2)(b) cannot adjudicate on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry or on the penalty, as it has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on the merits of the findings in a domestic enquiry. Those questions have to be adjudicated in a subsequent industrial dispute, if raised. [Para 37]

■

It is stated that one of the dismissed workmen, namely K, is no more. Since Union is representing the workmen, in case the award is passed by the Labour Court in favour of the workmen, the benefit flowing from the award shall accrue to the legal representatives of the deceased workman-K. [Para 38]

■

Hence, following order is passed: (i) Writ Petition is dismissed. (ii) The matter is remitted to the Labour Court to consider the challenge to the merits of the finding of the disciplinary enquiry as well as the penalty imposed. (iii) Parties shall appear before the Labour Court on 21.07.2025 without waiting for any notice. (iv) The records secured shall be sent back. [Para 39]

Even if the enquiry proceedings are held to be proper and the finding of misconduct is also accepted, the Tribunal has now power to consider whether the punishment of dismissal or discharge was necessary for the type of misconduct of which the workman is found guilty. In such circumstances, the Tribunal can also give any other relief to the workman, including the imposing of a lesser punishment." [Para 8.3]

■ From the analysis of Workmen of Firestone Tyre and Rubber Co. of India (P.) Ltd. v. Management ([1973] 1 SCC 813), it transpires that the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that there is an obligation on the part of employer to hold a proper enquiry before dismissing or discharging a workman. If, the management being fully aware of this decision of law does not conduct an enquiry or conduct a defective enquiry, the order passed by it is illegal and it cannot take advantage of such illegality or wrong committed by it and seek further opportunity before the Tribunal for adducing evidence for the first time. Then, it be permitted. [Para 8.4]

Section 11A read with its proviso if construed, would not only be in consonance with the intent of object of the Act, but also would be in consonance with the principles of interpretation of the statutes. Normally, a proviso is meant to be an exception to something within the main enactment or to qualify something enacted therein which but for the proviso would be within the purview of the enactment. In other words, a proviso cannot be torn apart from the main enactment nor can it be used to nullify or set at naught the real object of the main enactment. [Para 8.6]

It is also stipulated that when the Management relies upon the enquiry conducted and also simultaneously adduces evidence before the Tribunal, it is the duty of the Tribunal to first adjudicate on the legality and validity of the Domestic Enquiry and in the circumstance, the Tribunal holds the Domestic Enquiry to be valid, there is no requirement of considering the evidence adduced before it on merits. However, if the Tribunal holds the Domestic Enquiry to be not proper/valid, the Tribunal derives jurisdiction to decide on the merits and thereupon look into the evidence adduced by the Management in support of the action taken against the workman. To answer the issue, whenever the Labour Court, during the course of trial forms an opinion that the domestic enquiry has not been conducted in a free and fair manner, then the said issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue in order to provide an opportunity to the parties to express their willingness to let in additional evidence. This distinction is of paramount importance in the context of Section 11-A in order to preserve the right to defend the case between the parties. Respondent was acquitted of criminal charges by competent court on 28.04.1999 - Union thereafter raised an industrial dispute concerning termination and retrenchment benefits - Dispute was referred by appropriate Government for adjudication to CGIT - Whether obligation of employer to hold a domestic inquiry is not dispensed with merely because a criminal prosecution is launched - Held, yes - Whether since respondent was acquitted on benefit of doubt, in absence of a departmental inquiry or any evidence on record justifying termination, punitive action meted out by petitioner to respondent could not be upheld merely based on a criminal allegation which had not been substantiated - FACT: ■

The petitioner–BSNL (successor to the Telecommunication Department, Ulhasnagar) had engaged the respondent–workman as a casual labourer on a daily-rate, intermittent basis: during 1980, again from 1985 to 1989 with artificial breaks, and lastly from 01.08.1990 until 06.12.1992 on the muster roll. His services were terminated on 07.12.1992 without holding any inquiry or following principles of natural justice. The record showed he sought reinstatement by making representations after being released on bail in 1992 and again after acquittal, but these were not acted upon. He was acquitted of the criminal charges by the competent court on 28.04.1999. The Union thereafter raised an industrial dispute on 25.07.1999 concerning termination and retrenchment benefits. The original employer was taken over by BSNL on 01.10.2000. The dispute was referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication to the Central Government Industrial Tribunal No. 2, Mumbai under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act.

■

By Award dated 06.03.2003 in Reference No. 2/96 of 2000, the CGIT held the employer had failed to prove its case and directed reinstatement of the workman with continuity of service and full back wages for the period 06.12.1992 to 10.05.1999.

■

On writ petition to the High Court.

HEADNOTE: Section  11-A  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Procedure and powers of Labour Court - Whether whenever Labour Court, during course of trial, forms an opinion that domestic enquiry has not been conducted in a free and fair manner, said issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue in order to provide an opportunity to parties to express their willingness to let in additional evidence - Held, yes - Whether if Labour Court forms an opinion that domestic enquiry was conducted in a fair manner, then it is not necessary to decide issue as a preliminary issue and Labour Court may proceed with final award - Held, yes - Whether this distinction is of paramount importance in context of section 11-A in order to preserve right to defend case between parties - Held, yes - Whether where Management had expressed in its written statement its willingness to let in additional evidence, but Labour Court decided issue finally based on enquiry officer's report and documents and evidence produced without deciding fairness of domestic enquiry as a preliminary issue, opportunity to let in additional evidence was denied to Management and, therefore, matter was liable to be remanded back to Labour Court for deciding issue afresh after providing opportunity to Management to let in additional evidence - Held, yes [Paras 18 to 21]

FACT: ■

A dispute arose between the appellant–Management and its workmen following a strike. The Management issued a show cause notice on 11-5-2011, placed the workmen under suspension, and issued charge memoranda. A domestic enquiry was conducted in which the workmen participated. The Enquiry Officer held the charges proved, following which a second show cause notice dated 17-8-2011 was issued. The explanations submitted by the workmen were rejected and orders of removal from service were passed on 20-8-2011. Aggrieved thereby, the workmen raised industrial disputes in I.D. Nos. 33, 34, 35, 36 and 37 of 2011 before the Labour Court, Pondicherry.

■

Before the Labour Court, the Management, in its written statement, specifically reserved its right to adduce additional evidence in the event the domestic enquiry was held to be unfair or defective. The parties adduced oral and documentary evidence. However, the Labour Court did not decide the fairness of the domestic enquiry as a preliminary issue; instead, while passing the final award, it held that the enquiry was not conducted in a free and fair manner and ordered reinstatement of the workmen.

■

The Management challenged the awards in writ petitions under article 226, but the writ Court confirmed the Labour Court’s awards.

■

Aggrieved thereby, the Management preferred intra-Court appeals before the High Court.

HELD: ■

The factual scenario is not controverted between the parties. [Para 10]

■

Regarding the procedures to be followed, if the Management, while reserving their right in the written statement, that they may be permitted to let in additional evidence in the event of Labour Court holding that the domestic enquiry is not fair and proper, at what point of time such an opportunity must be allowed to be exercised by the Management is the issue for consideration. [Para 11]

■

Two circumstances may arise. If the Labour Court forms an opinion that the domestic enquiry has been conducted in a fair manner, then the Management is not entitled to let in additional evidence. In such a situation, there would be no impediment for the Labour Court to decide the issues and pass an award. In cases where, during the course of trial, the Labour Court forms an opinion that the domestic enquiry has not been conducted in a free and fair manner, the said issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue, enabling the parties to exercise their option to let in evidence in the context of section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The opportunity to let in additional evidence by the parties before the Labour Court is a valuable opportunity afforded under the Statute. In the event of Labour Court deciding the main issue without deciding the above preliminary issue, in such circumstances, the opportunity to let in additional evidence is denied and that is exactly the reason why the Courts have emphasised that if the domestic enquiry is found to be not fair and proper, then such an issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue and thereafter, either of the party may express their willingness to let in additional evidence to establish their case. In the event of not deciding the preliminary issue regarding the fairness of the enquiry, then the valuable opportunity to let in additional evidence is taken away. If the Labour Court decides that the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, the question of deciding the preliminary issue regarding the fairness of the enquiry does not arise at all. [Para 13]

■

Magistrate had yet not taken cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused named therein but merely had referred the complaint to the police for investigation and to file a challan/charge sheet if there was evidence. From the above, it was clear that there was no criminal proceeding pending so as to tantamount to a parallel proceeding as contended by the respondents. The application for stay was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. [Paras 14 and 15] The pleadings in the instant case were complete and no further disclosure was required to be made by the respondents against whom the criminal case was filed. Therefore, the arguments advanced by the respondents/applicants that they would be prejudiced by the continuance of the instant proceedings were without any basis and were not tenable. No prejudice was likely to affect them. Moreover, the CLB has consistently taken a view that if both the parties on similar grounds have filed another civil case, the CLB would not encourage parallel proceedings. There was nothing to prevent the CLB to proceed with the instant case when the criminal complaint filed was only at stage of investigation by the police. Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India [1970] 3 SCC 694, it can be said that the proceedings before the CLB can continue even when criminal case is pending which may have been filed by either parties against each other. The matters before the CLB are to be decided in summary proceedings on the basis of evidence by way of affidavits filed by the parties. The overall assessment of the case led to the conclusion that the CLB could proceed with the case when criminal proceedings were pending. However, there was no need to proceed in the instant case for the reasons that the whole issue was evolving around the question of 55,005 shares held by the petitioner which had been fraudulently and by tampering certain documents allegedly were reduced to 405 shares. The question of tampering the documents fraudulently or otherwise had to be decided by the Criminal Court. That being the sole basis of the petition, the case was to be adjourned sine-die with certain directions to be followed. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section  33  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of proceedings - Whether question as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper, if raised in an application under section 33(2)(b), and if finding on such an application is recorded after full fledged enquiry, such finding is not just a prima facie finding on said question as to fairness and validity of domestic enquiry and it is a finding on adjudication which attains finality if not questioned, and cannot be re-agitated in subsequent proceedings between same parties - Held, yes - Whether finding on issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory and said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging penalty - Held, yes - Whether thus, enquiry under section 33(2)(b) as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper (rendered after recording of evidence before authority) is binding on parties to proceeding as authority has jurisdiction to adjudicate on fairness of domestic enquiry and said finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute assailing order of penalty as it operates as res judicata between same parties in a subsequent proceeding - Held, yes - Whether however, authority under section 33(2)(b) cannot adjudicate on merits of finding in domestic enquiry or on penalty, as it has no jurisdiction to adjudicate on merits of findings in a domestic enquiry - Held, yes - Whether those questions have to be adjudicated in a subsequent industrial dispute, if raised - Held, yes [Paras 23, 35 and 37]

FACT: ■

Three members of the petitioner-Union were dismissed from service. The Management invoked section 33(2)(b) seeking approval for a penalty of dismissal. In the said proceeding, workmen took a stand that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper. Evidence was led on the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. The Labour Court, on appreciation of evidence led before it by both sides, held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper. Consequently, accorded approval for dismissal.

■

The Union later raised a dispute challenging the penalty of dismissal. Union contended that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper. The Management urged that in a proceeding under section 33(2)(b), it had already been held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper and the said finding operates as res judicata and cannot be agitated again, in a proceeding challenging penalty of dismissal of service.

■

The Labour Court accepted the Management’s plea and declined to reconsider the said issue, holding that it operates as res judicata.

■

On writ petition:

HELD: ■

The doctrine of Res judicata as a principle would also apply to proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is well settled and not disputed. To apply the principle of Res judicata contained in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in the context of the present case, the management has to satisfy the following: (a) the authority under section 33(2)(b) has the jurisdiction to adjudicate the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. (b) the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry decided earlier has attained finality. [Para 12]

■

There is no dispute that the said issue is considered in a proceeding under section 33(2)(b). The union contends that the said issue is not adjudicated and there is only a prima facie consideration of the point, while deciding the application under section 33(2)(b). [Para 13]

■

Scope of section 33(2)(b) is considered by the Apex Court in Lord Krishna Textile Mills v. Workmen. AIR 1961 SC 860 [Para 15]

■

In the said case, the Apex Court has held that if before dismissing an employee the employer has held a proper domestic enquiry and has proceeded to pass the impugned order as a result of the said enquiry, the authority has to satisfy that further requirements of section 33(2)(b) are satisfied. In other words, before embarking on the question as to whether the further requirements of section 33(2)(b) are complied or not, the Authority has to consider the question whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. Thus, it logically flows that to consider the compliance of section 33(2)(b), the Authority under section 33(2)(b) should also satisfy itself that the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. [Para 16]

■

at paragraph No. 21 of the written statement. The Petitioner further knew that three issues were framed and then also did not make any request that the validity of the Domestic Enquiry which was Issue No. 1 should be decided as a preliminary issue. [Para 37]

■

In that view of the matter, this Court cannot permit the petitioner to raise that objection to the impugned Award for not framing the preliminary issue, in the present proceedings. [Para 38]

■ Now taking note of the merits, in the previous segments of the instant judgment, this Court has duly taken note of what were the three issues which were framed on 2-5-2023. Issue No.1 specifically dealt with as to whether the Domestic Enquiry conducted by the Management was justifiable and was conducted by following the rules of natural justice. However, a perusal of the entire impugned Award shows that there is not a single whisper as regards the Issue No. 1 which pertains to the fairness of the Domestic Enquiry. The impugned Award shows that the Industrial Tribunal decided the other 2 issues. In the opinion of this Court, the impugned Award dated 20-1-2025 cannot be sustained in law without a decision in respect to the Issue No.1 inasmuch as without a decision in respect of Issue No. 1, the Tribunal could not have decided the Issue Nos. 2 and 3. [Para 39]

■

Accordingly, this Court has to set aside the impugned Award dated 20-1-2025 inasmuch as, when the Domestic Enquiry is being relied upon and an issue had been framed and no decision is rendered as regards the validity of the Domestic Enquiry, the said impugned Award cannot be sustained in law. [Para 40]

■

Accordingly, the instant writ petition stands disposed of with the following observations and directions: (i) The impugned Award dated 20-1-2025 passed in Reference Case No.04/2012 by the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh is set aside and quashed. (ii) The Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh is directed to decide afresh the said reference proceedings. (iii) Taking into account that the petitioner now has urged that the fairness of the Domestic Enquiry is required to be first decided, this Court directs the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh to first decide Issue No.1. (iv) Based upon the decision of Issue No.1, the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh shall thereupon decide the Issue Nos. 2 and 3. (v) It has been submitted at the bar that both the petitioner as well as the respondent No.1 would not be adducing any further evidence and as such, on the basis of the evidence which are already available on record, the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh shall do the needful as directed above. (vi) Taking into account that the respondent No.1 was dismissed from service in the year 2008, the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh shall decide the said dispute within a period of 6 (six) months from the date of appearance of both the parties before the Tribunal. (vii) As both the parties are duly present before this Court, they are directed to appear before the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh on 13-7-2026. (viii) The Registry is directed to intimate the Industrial Tribunal, Dibrugarh about the present judgment. (ix) Return the TCR forthwith and if necessary, the Registry shall employ the services of the Special Messenger so that the records are available before the learned Tribunal on the date fixed hereinabove for appearance of the parties.. [Para 41]

Shree Bharati Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. in T.C.P. No. 28/1997. This order of the Tribunal dt. 23rd Feb., 1999, in ITA No. 1601/Mds/98 in the case of M/s Suryaprabha Mills Ltd. was confirmed by the Hon'ble Madras High Court in TC No. 339 of 2000 by judgment, dt. 20th Feb., 2001, wherein their Lordships observed in para 3 that:

"On consideration, we find no substantial question of law is involved in this tax case. That apart, the controversy had already been set at rest by this Court by judgment, dt. 19th Dec., 1997, passed in TCP No. 28 of 1997 [CIT v. Shree Bharathi Cotton Mills (P) Ltd.] which has not been disputed by the learned standing counsel for the Department, in view of the above, this tax case is dismissed. No costs."

Therefore, we have decided to inspect Surya Prabha Mills (P) Ltd. to have a direct knowledge of its functioning to decide the issue, as agreed by both the sides to the dispute.

9. On inspection of the said mill and its function and production, it is found that the machineries replaced are not independent one from blow room to cone winding, various machines are functioning but none of them produce any material that has marketability. The functioning of one machine is depended upon the others comprised in the unit of the mill. After seeing this, we called for the production process chart from the mill authorities. Accordingly, they were furnished along with a note containing the process of manufacture, which are kept on record. For better appreciation, the note on process of manufacture as furnished, is extracted hereunder:

"Mixing : Raw material requires a homogeneous mixing to get the yarn in the desired quality and condition. It may be a composition of different varieties of cotton blended with or without the addition of reusable waste. Blow Room : This process involves opening of cotton and elimination of impurities such as trash, sand, seeds, etc. Cotton duly cleaned is collected in the form of uniform compressed sheets which is rolled into a lap. These laps have predetermined weight per unit length to meet the desired standard.

Carding : The impurities still lying in the laps and certain amount of short fibers are eliminated in this process, Individualisation and parallelisation of the fibers are effected by repeated brushing. The final product of carding is delivered in the form of sliver.

Combing : The carded slivers are fed into the sliver lapping machine to get sliver laps which are again drafted into ribbon laps. The ribbon laps are then combed by feeding into comber machines. Combing process is used for removing greater part of short fibres and for achieving a high degree of fibre parallelisation which is necessary for the spinning of high quality yarn.

Drawing : In this process several slivers received from carding and on combing are drawn and reduced to the thickness of one sliver by doubling and drafting to get improved blending and parallelisation of fibers. This process helps to enhance uniformity and strength of the yarn.

Simplex : The finished drawing sliver passes through a stage of processing called simplex. In this process, necessary drafts are employed to make the sliver into further thinner ends and a limited twist is applied to bind the fibers and then it is wound on bobbins as roves."

HEADNOTE: Section  11A  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, read with Rule 14 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 - Powers of Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals to give appro­priate relief in case of discharge or dismissal of workmen - Respondent-workman was employed in a defence organisation - He was charged with stealing brass and copper pieces - A departmental inquiry was initiated - On different dates, respondent did not appear; when he appeared, he admitted charges, and on subsequent dates he again remained absent - Inquiry officer submitted a report holding him guilty - After issuing notice, disciplinary authority imposed penalty of removal from service - CGIT held that termination was not proper and legal, quashed penalty of removal, and awarded compensation of Rs. 2.5 lakhs to respondent - In employer’s writ, High Court upheld quashing of removal order but gave liberty to proceed with inquiry from stage of express denial of charges, directed that reasonable opportunity be afforded to engage a defence assistant, and that inquiry be conducted under Rule 14 of CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965 - High Court quashed compensation, deemed workman to be under suspension till conclusion of inquiry, and directed that inquiry be concluded expeditiously and preferably within six months - Whether since respondent was given opportunity on a number of times and even, when he finally appeared and accepted charges, still on many dates, he did not appear resulting in inquiry report being submitted against him, order of CGIT as also impugned order passed by High Court were to be set aside and punishment awarded to respondent by Management was to be restored - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9]

FACT: ■

The respondent–workman, employed in a defence organisation (Gun Carriage Factory, Jabalpur), was charged with stealing brass and copper pieces. A departmental inquiry was initiated. On different dates the respondent did not appear; when he appeared, he admitted the charges, and on subsequent dates he again remained absent. The inquiry officer submitted a report holding him guilty. After issuing notice, the disciplinary authority imposed the penalty of removal from service.

■

The CGIT held that the termination was not proper and legal, quashed the penalty of removal, and awarded compensation of Rs. 2.5 lakhs to the respondent.

■

In the employer’s writ, the High Court upheld the quashing of the removal order but gave liberty to proceed with the inquiry from the stage of express denial of charges, directed that reasonable opportunity be afforded to engage a defence assistant, and that the inquiry be conducted under Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965. The High Court quashed the compensation, deemed the workman to be under suspension till conclusion of the inquiry, and directed that the inquiry be concluded expeditiously and preferably within six months.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the employer contended that the charges concerned theft in a defence factory; the respondent repeatedly remained absent; he had admitted the charges; the inquiry officer found him guilty; the disciplinary authority, after notice, removed him; and the CGIT exceeded its limited scope of interference, with compensation being unwarranted. The respondent contended he was coerced to accept the charges and that lack of a defence assistant led to miscarriage of justice.

HELD: ■

Court finds that the order passed by the CGIT and as held by the High Court vide its impugned order, cannot be sustained. [Para 7]

■

From the material available on record, it transpires that the appellant had been quite indulgent with the respondent during the inquiry as he was given opportunity on a number of times and even, when he finally appeared and accepted the charges, still on many dates, he did not appear resulting in the inquiry report being submitted against him. At this juncture, pausing to take note of the plea raised by counsel for the respondent that he had signed the document admitting the charges under duress and pressure, the same is noticed only to be rejected, the reason being that there could not have been any coercion because already the respondent was under suspension and thus, whatever action the appellant had to take, had been taken and more so, for the reason that there has been no representation or application from the respondent before any authority bringing on record the fact that he was coerced on the relevant date to admit to the charges. A second explanation has also been offered by the respondent that the respondent was under the impression that it was an inquiry report in his favour on which he had to sign, is self-contradictory to the earlier stand which also leads to the obvious presumption that neither of the defence is truthful. [Para 8]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  10  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Reference to Board, Court or Tribunal - Respondent-workmen were terminated from service by petitioner-employer on account of their participation in illegal strike - At instance of respondent-workmen, references were made by appropriate Government to Labour Court relating to termination of services of respondent-workmen - Labour Court held that departmental enquiry conducted against respondent-workmen was legal, fair and proper, however, findings recorded by Enquiry Officer were perverse - Whether since petitioner-employer had been able to prove only twin elements of charges namely, (i) gathering at gate by leaving work, and (ii) insubordination/indiscipline and disorderly behaviour, order passed by Labour Court was to be interfered with only partly while upholding same with regard to charge of unauthorised absence - Held, yes [Paras 28 and 29]

FACT: ■

The petitioner was engaged in the business of manufacturing compact fin heat exchangers, plate heat exchangers, single tube heat exchangers, transformer cooling system etc. and also provided solutions to various industries, including transportation, energy, oil, gas etc. The respondents were working with the petitioner in various positions as workmen.

■

It was alleged that on 19-2-2020, office bearers of a union called upon the workmen to gather at the gate of the factory. Instead of starting the work and performing normal duties, the workmen gathered in front of the gate of the factory. The Managing Director of the company attempted to pacify the union leaders, as well as the entire mob of the workmen and repeatedly requested them not to resort to any indiscipline and to commence the work. However, the mob of the workmen refused to act on the request of the Managing Director and later became violent. It was alleged that the mob broke glasses, threw stones on the bus and security cabin. The company was left with no option but to call the police. The crowd went on rampage till arrival of the police. The police disbursed the mob and arrested the union leader and few others.

■

It was alleged that since 20-2-2020, the respondent-workmen did not report for work. It was alleged that the acts committed by the respondent-workmen amounted to illegal strike causing unprecedented damage and loss to the company. It was alleged that the respondent workmen committed serious misconduct under Clauses 24(a), 24(b), 24(k) and 24(l) of the Model Standing Orders.

■

The respondent-workmen submitted their respective replies to the chargesheets. The supplementary chargesheet was issued alleging unauthorised absence from 20-2-2020 and misconduct under Clause 24(f) of the Model standing orders. By the supplementary chargesheet, a practising advocate was also appointed as Enquiry Officer.

■

The Enquiry Officer conducted enquiry and submitted report holding that misconduct under Clauses 24(a), (k), (l) and (f) was fully proved. The misconduct alleged under Clause 24(b) was held to be disproved.

■

The petitioner passed orders dismissing the respondent-employees from service based on the findings of the Enquiry Officer. At the instance of the respondents, References were made by the appropriate Government to Labour Court relating to termination of services of the respondent-workmen under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

■

The respondent-workmen filed their Statements of Claim, which were resisted by filing Written Statements by the petitioner-employer. The Labour Court proceeded to frame preliminary issues relating to fairness in the enquiry and perversity in the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer.

■

The Labour Court held that departmental enquiry conducted against the respondent-workmen is legal, fair and proper. However, it held that the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer to the extent of charges under Clauses (a), (k), (l) and (f) of MSO, 2024 are perverse.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

The petitioner-employer has been able to prove only the twin elements of charges namely, (i) gathering at the gate by leaving work, and (ii) insubordination/indiscipline and disorderly behaviour. The charge of unauthorised absence under Clause-24(f) of the Model Standing Orders is not proved. Therefore, the order passed by the Labour Court deserves to be interfered with only partly while upholding the same with regard to the charge of unauthorised absence. [Para 28]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  25-T,  read with section  25-U,  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Prohibition of unfair labour practice - An incident occurred at Borjan Tea Estate where a mob of workers forcefully entered factory, damaged property and pelted stones, resulting in injuries to Manager - Eleven workmen were charge-sheeted for gross misconduct and were dismissed from service - Government of Assam referred dispute to Labour Court on whether management was justified in dismissing workmen - Labour Court upheld legality and validity of domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld dismissal of workmen - Whether Labour Court ought to have framed a preliminary issue on legality and validity of domestic enquiries held against workmen - Held, yes - Whether Labour Court, after upholding domestic enquiries held against workmen, ought to have decided as regards proportionality of punishments which had been imposed against workmen - Held, yes - Whether since Enquiry Officer did not even care to give reasons as to why action was taken only against workmen, enquiry reports were in conflict with principles of natural justice, and were also perverse - Held, yes - Whether Labour Court ought to have rejected reports of domestic enquiries and proceeded to decide on merits on basis of evidence which was available - Held, yes - Whether therefore, instant case was a fit case for exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 of Constitution to interfere with Award passed in Reference Case No. 02/2009 and to remand matter to Labour Court to decide Reference on merits - Held, yes [Paras 22, 24, 31, 32, 33 and 34]

FACT: ■

The dispute arose from an incident at Borjan Tea Estate in March 2007 when around 1,500 workers gathered at the factory gate; some forcefully entered, damaged office property, pelted stones, and the Manager sustained injuries, following which the Estate remained under lockout for 11 days. Eleven workmen were charge-sheeted for forming an unlawful assembly, instigating violence and damage to garden property, with alleged loss of about Rs. 19.66 lakhs, and were charged with gross misconduct under the Estate Standing Orders. The workmen denied involvement; the gateman stated the gate was broken by some workers after overpowering him. Separate domestic enquiries were conducted against each of the 11 workmen and enquiry reports held them guilty of gross misconduct. The management issued notices seeking representations; after time extension, no representations were submitted, and the workmen were dismissed from service, the Reference later describing dismissal as with effect from 10.09.2007.

■

Following the dismissal, the Government of Assam referred the dispute to the Labour Court, Dibrugarh, on whether the management was justified in dismissing the 11 named workmen and, if not, whether they were entitled to reinstatement with back wages. In its written statement, the management relied on the domestic enquiries as the basis for dismissal and reserved the right to adduce evidence on merits if the enquiries were found violative of natural justice. The workmen, in their written statement, asserted that the enquiries were not impartial, that they were denied opportunity to adduce defence evidence, and that the Presenting Officer for the management also acted as a witness; they denied instigating or participating in the violence.

■

The Labour Court proceeded to record evidence without first framing a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries. The proceedings initially went ex parte against the workmen; the management submitted evidence-in-chief and later stated it would not adduce further evidence. Management witnesses were cross-examined and the workmen also adduced evidence. The Enquiry Officer (examined as M.W. 4) stated in cross-examination that although workmen were informed of the enquiry and to participate, he did not inform them that they were required to adduce evidence, stating that the Presenting Officer would inform them. The records of the domestic enquiries were not placed before the Labour Court. The Head Clerk (examined as M.W. 2), whose evidence had formed the basis of the domestic findings, admitted in cross-examination that he did not remember the names of the workers involved in the incident. The enquiry reports recorded that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and did not give reasons for proceeding only against these 11 workmen.

■

By Award dated 29.02.2016 in Reference Case No. 02/2009, the Labour Court upheld the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld the dismissal of the workmen; no separate finding on proportionality of the punishment was recorded.

■

On writ petition to the High Court.

HELD: ■

1992 to 10.05.1999.

■

On writ petition to the High Court.

HELD: ■

The facts on record indicate that the Respondent had admittedly worked intermittently with the Telecommunication Department, Ulhasnagar, from 1980 onwards. His last period of engagement was from 01.08.1990 till 06.12.1992, on the Muster Roll prior to his arrest on allegation of theft. [Para 8]

■ It is undisputed that the Respondent was arrested on 06.12.1992 and he was terminated from service forthwith without any inquiry on the following day, i.e., 07.12.1992. No inquiry was conducted; principles of natural justice were not followed prior to termination. The record reflects that the Respondent workman got bail and gave letters for his reinstatement in 1992 itself, but the Petitioners ignored the same. Thereafter, he was acquitted from the criminal charge by the Competent Court on 28.04.1999 and he once again approached the Petitioners, who ignored him. [Para 9]

■

Despite the Petitioner's contentions, the Tribunal has rightly held that termination without inquiry, especially when allegations are serious and criminal proceedings are pending, is unsustainable. The obligation of the employer to hold a domestic inquiry is not dispensed with merely because a criminal prosecution is launched. The Petitioner has failed to demonstrate any compliance with the procedure under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and no material is placed before the Court to justify non-adherence thereto. [Para 10]

■

The Tribunal has also considered the Petitioner's argument regarding delay and laches. The record shows that the Respondent sent representations immediately after being released on bail and again in 1999 post his acquittal but was intentionally ignored by the Petitioner. The Union took up his cause shortly thereafter. The Court found no gross negligence or inaction on the part of the Respondent to deny relief solely on the ground of delay. On these facts, the grievance of the Petitioner on the ground of delay is unacceptable. [Para 11]

■

The argument that the Respondent was not a member of the Union which raised the dispute is also devoid of merit. It is well settled that a Union may espouse the cause of a workman even without formal membership, if done with his consent or in the larger interest of the workmen. The Tribunal has correctly applied the legal maxim of espousal and its findings are consistent with settled principles of industrial jurisprudence. [Para 12]

■

The Petitioner further contends that acquittal was not on merits but by giving him benefit of doubt, and therefore, reinstatement should not automatically follow. However, in the absence of a departmental inquiry or any evidence on record justifying termination, this Court cannot uphold the punitive action meted out by the Petitioners to the Respondent merely based on a criminal allegation which has not been substantiated. Further, the Respondent stands cleared of all charges. [Para 13]

■

The submission regarding the Respondent's employment status being "daily-rated" and hence disentitling him to relief is also rejected in view of the aforesaid findings that he admittedly worked from 1980 to 1992 with the Petitioners. The Tribunal has taken into account the pattern of the Respondent's employment and found continuity in engagement sufficient to attract the protection of the Industrial Disputes Act, which the Court is unable to dislodge. [Para 14]

■

On the basis of the above, no case is made out to interfere with the well-reasoned and cogent Award passed by the Tribunal. The Writ Petition is devoid of merit and stands dismissed. The Respondent has expired in the interregnum. Hence, under the Award, the dues would have to be paid over to Respondent Nos. 1A to 1F, equally i.e., in equal proportion, forthwith. [Para 15]

■

All parties, including the Registry of this Court, shall act on a server copy of this order downloaded from the website of the High Court. The Respondent's Advocate shall forthwith provide the details of Respondent Nos. 1A to 1F viz., self-attested Aadhaar card copy, self-attested bank account details and passbook copy with IFSC Code, etc., and any other details as required by the Registry of this Court. [Para 16]

■

By order dated 12.12.2005, this Court (Coram: V.C. Daga, J.) directed the Petitioners to deposit the entire back wages from 06.12.1992 amounting to Rs.6,10,137/-, which was deposited by the Petitioners in this Court on 13.02.2006. [Para 17]

■

held before the Tribunal. Based on fresh enquiry before the Tribunal, the issues relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry and the merit of the charges were adjudicated. However, in the instant case, the enquiry was held to be valid, and later the order on termination was approved. There is no adjudication on the merits of the charges when the issue relating to the fairness of the enquiry was considered. Thus, the said judgment does not apply to the fact situation. [Para 25]

■ The union has relied on the judgments of the Division Bench of this Court in The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company Ltd. v. Workmen1975 LAB I C 879 and RPG Cables Limited v. G.M. Kulkarni [WA NO.600 of 2012 (L-RES), dated 26.11.2012] to contend that under section 33(2)(b), there is no jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute. [Para 26]

■

In The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company and RPG Cables supra, the Division Bench of this Court has referred to the judgment in Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra, and this Court has already discussed the said judgment. This Court is of the view that the judgment in Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra does not lay down a law, that a finding under section 33(2)(b), holding the domestic enquiry as fair and proper, (that too after recording evidence in section 33(2)(b) proceeding), can be re-agitated in an Industrial dispute. [Para 27]

■

Moreover, it is not forthcoming from the facts in The Management of Amalgamated Electric Company supra as to whether any evidence was recorded by the parties on an application under section 33(2)(b). [Para 28]

■

More than anything else, paragraph No.19 of the judgment of the Apex Court in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills v. PT. Ram Sarup AIR 1957 SC 82(4 Judges bench) dealt with section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 which in substance is pari materia with section 33 when it comes to nature of enquiry is not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 30]

■

The aforementioned paragraph would lead to the inevitable conclusion that while exercising jurisdiction under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal Act), 1950 which is similar to section 33 when it comes to the nature of enquiry, the authority has to consider whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper and then, has to proceed to decide as to whether approval sought is to be granted or not by considering other requirements. This being the position, the jurisdiction of the authority under section 33, is adjudicatory on the question whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper. Though the judgment in Lakshmidevi Sugar Mills supra is quoted in RPG Cables supra, it appears paragraphs extracted above are not brought to the notice of the Division Bench of this Court. [Para 31]

■

The said judgement would lead to the conclusion that while dealing with an application under section 33(2)(b) of Act, 1947 if the authority gives a finding and holds that the enquiry was not fair and proper and thereafter permits the parties to lead evidence afresh on the charges levelled, then in such situation the defect in enquiry gets cured. In such an event, in a subsequent proceeding under section 10, there cannot be any further enquiry relating to the fairness of the disciplinary enquiry. [Para 32]

■

Though judgments in G. McKenzie and Punjab National Bank Ltd. supra at the first glance indicate that the jurisdiction under section 33(2)(b) is limited to consider prima facie aspects and not adjudicatory, on consideration of the factual background in which those judgments are rendered one cannot but conclude that jurisdiction exercised while refusing or granting approval under section 33(2)(b), is adjudicatory on few aspects namely, "Whether the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, which in its fold may include few aspects like, compliance of principles of natural justice, compliance of requirements of the Standing Orders governing domestic enquiry or compliance of any other binding contract of employment, payment of wages as provided under section 33(2)(b)?" [Para 33]

■

After considering the above aspects, if the Authority takes a final call approving the punishment imposed, then the order granting approval for the punishment is neither an adjudication on the merits of the finding in the domestic enquiry nor on the proportionality of the punishment. It is in this context, it has been held that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited to lifting the ban on the punishment. [Para 34]

■

The interpretation that the scope of enquiry under section 33(2)(b) is limited cannot be stretched to contend that the finding as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper is not on adjudication. For the reasons recorded above, it is held that the finding on the issue relating to fairness of domestic enquiry is adjudicatory. HELD: In P. Jayappan v. S.K. In the case of Shambu Nath Goyal v. In the said case, before the Supreme Court, the facts as would appear was that pursuant to an industrial dispute, Reference was made by the Central Government to the Industrial Tribunal, Chandigarh. The Management filed the written statement on 12.08.1970 contending that the dispute was not an industrial dispute. FACT: ■

The petitioner–Management had initiated disciplinary action against the respondent–workman following a complaint that he used abusive language and physically attacked a co-employee, who underwent hospital treatment and lodged an FIR. The respondent was suspended pending enquiry. A charge memo with four charges of assault, intimidation, and use of abusive language was issued. The Management filed an application under Section 33(2)(b) seeking approval of the termination and paid approximately Rs. 0.52 lakhs towards final settlement along with one month’s wages. The Deputy Commissioner of Labour (Conciliation II) approved the termination. It was recorded that no evidence was adduced before the approving authority, though the approval order discussed the allegations, material from the domestic enquiry, and recorded conclusions on the facts.

Challenging the termination, the respondent invoked Section 2A. As no order was passed within 45 days, the dispute was filed before the Additional Labour Court as O.P. No. 145 of 2023. The respondent filed a memo seeking a preliminary decision on the fairness of the domestic enquiry. By order dated 9/10/2024, the Labour Court treated the approving authority as a quasi-judicial authority not superior to the Labour Court, noted that parties had let in evidence and were cross-examined before the approving authority, treated the approving authority’s finding on the correctness of the domestic enquiry as beyond jurisdiction and a nullity, and directed the Management to adduce evidence afresh on the preliminary issue of fairness of the domestic enquiry.

The nature of allegations and the authorities before whom the same are levelled may determine the gravity of misconduct. As of now, this Court is not going into the issue of seriousness of misconduct. ■ It cannot be contended that findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer relating to second charge are based on absolutely no evidence. The Enquiry Officer has considered evidence before it. [Para 25]

■

In domestic enquiry the test for proof of charge is preponderance of probability. It is not necessary to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt. It is not for the Labour or Industrial Courts to comment on quality or quantity of evidence. So long as there is some evidence on record to support findings of the Enquiry Officer, Labour and Industrial Courts cannot go into aspect of adequacy of evidence. [Para 26]

■

Thus, in a domestic enquiry the strict and sophisticated rules of Indian Evidence Act do not apply. Any material which is logically probative for a prudent man can be taken into consideration by the Enquiry Officer. So long as there is some evidence on record, however compendious it may be, the same can be relied upon for recording finding of guilt. It is only in a case involving total absence of evidence that a finding can be treated as perverse. [Para 28]

■

In the present case, it is difficult to hold that there is absolutely no evidence to prove the allegations in the two charges levelled against the respondent. The Labour and Industrial Courts have failed to appreciate well settled principles relating to test of preponderance of probability for proving charges in the domestic enquiry. [Para 29]

■

Considering the overall conspectus of the case, Court is of the view that the Labour and the Industrial Courts have grossly erred in holding that the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer are perverse. The impugned orders of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court qua preliminary issue relating to perversity therefore are unsustainable and liable to be set aside. [Para 30]

■

However, though the impugned orders of Labour and Industrial Courts qua the preliminary issue of perversity are being set aside, this does not mean that the order of punishment will have to be necessarily upheld. By setting aside the impugned orders, all that is being prevented is need for the Bank to lead evidence to prove the charges before the Labour Court. The charges are correctly held to be proved in the enquiry. The Labour Court would now proceed to determine whether punishment of dismissal imposed on the respondent is legal and is proportionate to the gravity of misconduct committed by her. Court has already held that the allegation in the first charge relating to misbehaviour with Mr. Bhat is not proved against the respondent. The Labour Court shall accordingly go into the issue of proportionality and decide the issue of correctness of punishment of dismissal uninfluenced by any of the findings recorded by this Court in the present judgment. [Para 31]

HELD: ■ It has been repeatedly held that proceedings under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 are only summary in nature and the Conciliation Officer does not decide the legality of the dismissal. The scope of the Conciliation Officer during an 'approval' consideration is confined to the following, in accordance with the judgment of the Supreme Court in Lalla Ram v. D.C.M. Chemical Works Ltd. [1979] 1978 taxmann.com 246 (SC)/(1978) 3 SCC 1. The Supreme Court at para 12 held as under:- "The position that emerges from the above quoted decisions of this Court may be stated thus: In proceedings under section 33(2)(b) of the Act, the jurisdiction of the industrial Tribunal is confined to the enquiry as to (i) whether a proper domestic enquiry in accordance with the relevant rules/Standing Orders and principles of natural justice has been held; (ii) whether a prima facie case for dismissal based on legal evidence adduced before the domestic tribunal is made out; (iii) whether the employer had come to a bona fide conclusion that the employee was guilty and the dismissal did not amount to unfair labour practice and was not intended to victimise the employee regard being had to the position settled by the decisions of this Court in Bengal Bhatdee Coal Co, v. Ram Probesh Singh(1), Titaghur Paper Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ram Naresh Kumar (2), Hind Construction & Engineering Co. Ltd. v. Their Workmen (3), Workmen of Messrs Firestone Tyre & Rubber Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Management & Ors (4), and Eastern Electric and Trading Co. v. Baldev Lal (5) that though generally speaking the award of punishment for misconduct under the Standing Orders is a matter for the management to decide and the Tribunal is not required to consider the propriety or adequacy of the punishment or whether it is excessive or too severe yet an inference of mala fides may in certain cases be drawn from the imposition of unduly harsh, severe, unconscionable or shockingly disproportionate punishment; (iv) whether the employer has paid or offered to pay wages for one month to the employee and (v) whether the employer has simultaneously or within such reasonably short time as to form part of the game transaction applied to the authority before which the main industrial dispute is pending for approval of the action taken by him. If these conditions are satisfied, the Industrial Tribunal would grant the approval which would relate back to the date from which the employer had ordered the dismissal. If however, the domestic enquiry suffers from any defect or infirmity, the labour authority will have to find out on its own assessment of the evidence adduced before it whether there was justification for dismissal and if it so finds it will grant approval of the order of dismissal which would also relate back to the date when the order was passed provided the employer had paid or offered to pay wages for one month to the employee and the employer had within the time indicated above applied to the authority before which the main industrial dispute is pending for approval of the action taken by him." The findings of the Deputy Commissioner has to be limited to grant or refusal of the Approval Application on the basis of the above directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Lalla Ram's case. [Para 13]
