HEADNOTE: Section  33,  read with section  20,  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Conditions of service to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of proceedings - Whether proceedings before Tribunal are deemed to continue until date on which award becomes enforceable under Section 17A - Held, yes - Whether where award recording settlement, disposal or other closure has been made, legal pendency under Section 20(3) does not vanish because parties may feel that dispute has ended - Held, yes - Whether once it is held that proceedings were pending in eye of law on relevant date, compliance with Section 33(2)(b) became obligatory if employer intended to dismiss workman for misconduct not connected with dispute - Held, yes - Whether where termination of workman was effected during pendency of References and was in contravention of Section 33(2)(b), workman was to be reinstated in service to his original post, or to an equivalent post carrying same pay scale, status and service benefits, with continuity of service for all purposes including seniority, increments and retiral benefits, subject to applicable rules - Held, yes - Whether workman was to be entitled to full back wages from date of termination till commencement of grocery shop in 2016, fifty percent back wages for period from 2016 till closure of grocery shop during Covid period and full back wages thereafter till date of reinstatement - Held, yes [Paras 27, 28, 30, 39 and 40]

FACT: ■

A charge-sheet dated 12 October 2012 was issued to the workman alleging misconduct under various Standing Orders. A domestic enquiry was conducted, and on 31 July 2014 the Enquiry Officer held the workman guilty; the report was forwarded on 6 October 2014. The workman submitted an apology on 16 October 2014, and the recognised Union also requested a sympathetic view. An industrial dispute was pending between the company and the recognised Union, and during its subsistence an MoU dated 14 August 2014 was executed stating that 13 of 18 suspended workmen would be taken back subject to conditions at the management’s discretion, while enquiries against the remaining five, including the workman, would continue. After considering the apology and the Union’s request, management decided to dismiss the workman, and he was terminated on 17 October 2014.

■

It was pleaded that he remained unemployed for about two years, then started a grocery business, and that the business suffered losses and was closed on 28 November 2021, after which he remained without gainful employment.

■

The workman filed a complaint under Section 33A challenging the dismissal as arbitrary and illegal and sought reinstatement with back wages, also alleging discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis 13 similarly situated workmen who were given minor punishment. By order dated 27 September 2019 on preliminary issues, the Tribunal held the domestic enquiry fair and proper and the findings not perverse.

■

By final Award dated 18 January 2024, the Tribunal declined reinstatement with back wages and awarded compensation of Rs. 7 lakhs, while recording that the termination occurred during pendency of References and thus amounted to breach of Section 33(2)(b).

■

On writ petitions before the High Court.

HELD: ■

Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is enacted as a provision of protection, made by Legislature with intention to preserve industrial peace during time when conciliation proceedings or adjudication proceedings are pending before competent authority. The object behind such provision is that when dispute between employer and workmen has reached legal forum, atmosphere between parties remains strained. At such stage, if employer is permitted to alter service conditions against workers, then pending proceedings may get influenced by pressure. Therefore, law intervenes and places temporary restraint upon employer's powers. In that sense, Section 33 is a statutory device for maintaining fairness. It keeps pending proceedings free from coercion. [Para 23]

■

Sub-section (1) of Section 33 deals with matters which are connected with pending industrial dispute. In such matters, Act requires prior permission in writing from authority before whom proceeding is pending. This shows that where subject matter of proposed action touches the dispute under consideration, employer cannot act and then justify later. Sub-section (2), however, addresses another category, namely matters not connected with pending dispute. There Act gives wider liberty to employer to proceed according to standing orders or contractual terms. Yet even there, if employer proposes discharge or dismissal of workman concerned in dispute, proviso imposes two mandatory pre-conditions. One month wages must be paid, and application for approval must be made before competent authority. Hence, even where misconduct is outside dispute, disciplinary power is not uncontrolled. [Para 24]

■

HEADNOTE: Section  25-T  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Unfair labour practices -  Prohibition of  - Petitioner, an employee of respondent-power distribution company, was dismissed from service solely on ground of registration of an offence under Prevention of Corruption Act - Petitioner filed a complaint before Labour Court - Respondent filed its written statement before Labour Court - On perusal of record, there were no averments explaining impracticability of holding an enquiry and no express reservation in written statement seeking permission to lead evidence before Court to prove misconduct - Labour Court allowed complaint and directed respondent to reinstate petitioner with 50 per cent back wages - Respondent filed revision before Industrial Court - Industrial Court allowed revision and remanded matter to Labour Court with a direction to frame an additional issue on whether respondent proved alleged charges of misconduct before Court - Whether since no domestic enquiry was held and employer had not, in its written statement, expressly reserved right to lead such evidence, Industrial Court was not justified in remanding matter to Labour Court to permit employer to prove misconduct by framing an additional issue - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order passed by Industrial Court was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8, 9.1 and 11]

FACT: ■

The petitioner, an employee of the respondent–power distribution company, was issued a show-cause notice after registration of a corruption offence alleging demand of Rs. 3,000. He denied the allegations. No departmental enquiry was initiated or conducted, and he was dismissed from service solely on the ground of registration of the offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act. He filed Complaint (ULP) No. 50 of 2014 before the Labour Court.

■

The respondents filed their written statement before the Labour Court. On perusal of the record, there were no averments explaining impracticability of holding an enquiry and no express reservation in the written statement seeking permission to lead evidence before the Court to prove misconduct.

■

The respondents filed Revision (ULP) No. 59 of 2017. The Industrial Court allowed the revision, set aside the Labour Court’s order dated 05.01.2017 in Complaint (ULP) No. 50 of 2014, and remanded the matter with a direction to frame an additional issue on whether the respondents proved the alleged charges of misconduct before the Court.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

HELD: ■

Having heard the counsel for the respective parties and upon perusal of the dismissal order, the complaint, the written statement, the order passed by the Labour Court in the earlier round of litigation, as well as the orders passed by the Industrial Court and the Labour Court after remand and upon going through the written statement filed by the respondents, it is evident that admittedly no departmental inquiry was initiated or conducted against the petitioner. The petitioner came to be dismissed from service solely on the ground of registration of an offence under the said Act. There are no averments in the written statement to the effect that, in the facts and circumstances of the case, it was not possible for the respondents to initiate or conduct an inquiry, whether due to fear or nonavailability of witnesses. The fact remains that the dismissal order was issued merely on the ground that an offence under the said Act was registered, and on that basis it was alleged that the image of the respondents was tarnished. As regards the contention raised by the counsel for the petitioner that the respondents had not reserved any right in their written statement to prove the charges by seeking a de novo inquiry before the Court, the Court, with the assistance of both the counsel, has perused the written statement (Exhibit-J, pages 59 to 67 of the paper-book), particularly through the additional facts and say filed by the respondents at Page No.63. [Para 7]

■

Authority of India Ltd. (supra). The order is purely administrative in nature. It is passed at a preliminary/preparatory stage and it is passed at a pre-enquiry stage as held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Steel Authority of India Ltd. (supra). In the considered opinion of this Court, merely because an opportunity of hearing was not given to the appellants, it does not vitiate the order passed by the CCI. [Para 38] A limited issue relating to an order passed under section 26(1) by the CCI setting the machinery in motion for conducting an enquiry by the Director General is dealt with and therefore, as the enquiry is yet to commence, wherein all grounds raised in the present petitions/appeals can be looked into, hence, the present petitions/appeals are premature. [Para 40]

In the considered opinion of this Court, the order passed in the case of All India Online Vendors Association v. Flipkart India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 100 taxmann.com 170 does not help the present appellants. The order was passed by the CCI on 6-11-2018 directing closure of the case under section 26(2) of the Act of 2002. The present order has been passed by the CCI under section 26(1) of the Act of 2002 on 13-1-2021, meaning thereby after a lapse of considerable long time it has been passed and in a competitive market various agreements are executed, new practices are adopted every day and merely because some other issue has been looked into by the CCI earlier, it does not mean that on the ground of res judicata the CCI cannot look into any information subsequently against the appellants. The principle of res judicata has no application in the matter under the Act of 2002 in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case. The market place is by its very nature a constantly evolving and dynamic space. The market forces can evolve even in the course of a few months and therefore, by no stretch of imagination, it can be held that the appellants should be out of bound for all times and no action can be taken against them only because at some point of time the matter has been looked into by the CCI. [Para 42]

In the considered opinion of this Court, an expert body cannot be crippled or hamstrung in their efforts by application of technical rules of procedure. [Para 44]

It can be safely gathered that by no stretch of imagination the order passed by the CCI under section 26(1) is going to cause harm to the business reputation of the appellants. [Para 46]

In the light of the aforesaid, in the considered opinion of this Court, by no stretch of imagination, the process of enquiry can be crushed at this stage. In case, the appellants are not at all involved in violation of any statutory provisions of Act of 2002, they should not feel shy in facing an enquiry. On the contrary, they should welcome such an enquiry by the CCI. The writ petitions filed against the order dated 13-1-2021 and the present writ appeals are nothing but an attempt to ensure that the action initiated by the CCI under the Act of 2002 does not attain finality and the same is impermissible in law as the Act of 2002 itself provides the entire mechanism of holding an enquiry, granting an opportunity of hearing, passing of a final order as well as appeal against the order passed by the CCI. In the considered opinion of this Court, the present writ appeals filed by the appellants are devoid of merits and substance, hence, deserve to be dismissed and are accordingly, dismissed. [Para 47]

headnotes.text: It is desirable that if the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry is being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending the final disposal of the criminal case. It would be particularly appropriate to adopt such a course where the charge against the workman is of a grave character, because in such a case, it would be unfair to compel the workman to disclose the defence which he may take before the criminal court. But to say that domestic enquiries may be stayed pending criminal trial is very different from anything that if an employer proceeds with the domestic enquiry in spite of the fact that the criminal trial is pending, the enquiry for that reason alone is vitiated and the conclusion reached in such an enquiry is either bad in law or mala fide.

In the instant case it was held that the Industrial Tribunal was in error when it characterised the result of the domestic enquiry as mala fide partly because the enquiry was not stayed pending the criminal proceedings against the concerned workman.

There is no legal prohibition which prevents the holding of a domestic enquiry into an act of misconduct by a workman just because a criminal case is pending against the workman. The domestic enquiry in which the workman is answerable to his master and which may end in a departmental penalty is entirely different from the criminal proceeding in which the same person in respect of the same act is prosecuted for violation of the penal law of the land, which may end in conviction and sentence.
Domestic enquiry—Pendency of Criminal case or appeal—Employer need not wait for its decision—Enquiry may be proceeded with.

The decision to hold or not to hold a domestic enquiry, during the pendency of a criminal trial in respect of the same allegation, against a workman, is that of the employer to be taken at his discretion and if the employer decides to hold such enquiry, he cannot be prevented from doing so by the issue of a writ of prohibition.

Held, that it was desirable that when the incident giving rise to a charge framed against a workman in a domestic enquiry was being tried in a criminal court, the employer should stay the domestic enquiry pending final disposal of the criminal case. In view of the accepted principles of law, in the event thepetitioner was convicted in the criminal trial, he would automatically be dismissed and/or removed from service, without taking recourse to formalities of departmental proceedings and, in the atternative, if the criminal case failed for want of evidence, by an order of discharge and not acquittal, in that event also, the departmental authorities would be entitled to proceed with the departmental enquiry, even after passing of such order of discharge by the criminal court. Therefore, during the pendency of the criminal trial, the employer would be restrained from proceeding further with the departmental enquiry against the petitioner.

The workmen were not dismissed from service on the ground of conviction in criminal proceedings. The workmen were dismissed from service on the basis of domestic enquiry, which is held vitiated on the ground of breach of natural justice. Without even getting a fair opportunity of being represented in the inquiry proceedings, the workmen were dismissed from service. Thus, action of the Employer is held to be unjustified.

A writ in the nature of prohibition preventing the holding of a domestic enquiry by an employer into alleged acts of misconduct by a workman can be issued only if there was total lack of jurisdiction in the authority holding the enquiry. No such writ can be issued preventing an authority having jurisdiction to hold the enquiry, even if criminal proceedings are pending in respect of the same matter.
The principles of natural justice do not require that the employer must wait for the decision of a criminal case or an appeal before proceeding with a domestic enquiry. 1960(1) L.L.J. 520, Approved.

Domestic enquiry—Company examining no witness nor producing any document in support of its case—Simply examining concerned workmen and cross-examining him—Such an enquiry is not proper and fair as contemplated by law.

An enquiry was conducted by a committee of 2 officers of the company. The workmen were found guilty and removed from employment. The Tribunal held that the termination was bad as the Manager who passed the order was the prosecutor and the judge.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry against workman—Pendency of criminal proceeding against workman no bar to domestic enquiry—Writ of prohibition against holding of domestic enquiry—Will issue only when there is total lack of jurisdiction.

Where a Criminal Court acquits an accused delinquent workman on the ground that evidence was not sufficient even to frame a charge and that the prosecution had not made out a case which, if unrebutted, would warrant the conviction of the accused, it would be a bar to the enquiry officer proceeding with a domestic enquiry for misconduct on the very same charge : K. Rangarajan v. State of Madras, [1966] 30 FJR 199 ; Anglo-American Direct Tea Trading Co. v. Industrial Tribunal, [1970] I LLJ 481, Workmen of Ruby Rubber Works v. Ruby Rubber Works, [1970] 37 FJR 514 and W.S. Insulators of India v. Mohd. Moosa, (1979) Lab IC 102, distinguished. Parry’s Confectionary Ltd. v. Industrial Tribunal, Madras, [1974] 45 FJR 329, Tirunelveli-Tuticorin Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. Industrial Tribunal, Madras, [1975] I LLJ 304 and Tirunelveli-Tuticorin Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. Industrial Tribunal, Madras, [1975] I LLJ 312, applied.
Domestic enquiry—Scope of power of Labour Court—Examination of witnesses—Duty of workman to properly summon witnesses—Failure of workman to do so—Enquiry held not improper.

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947—Sections 11-A and 25-F—Dismissal—Upheld by Labour Court—Hence, instant petition—Allegation upon workmen was to set fire to the officer of Tea Estate inside to his car after beating him badly—Held, allegation of no proper enquiry proceeding unsustainable—Entire proceedings of the domestic enquiry was placed before the Labour Court which were examined—There was no denial regarding the said documents by the petitioner Sangha in its written statement—Mere acquittal in criminal case would not absolve the workmen from the charges—Acquittal was on the basis of doubt—Allegation of no opportunity of cross-examination and not providing the copy of enquiry report could not be established by petitioner-Sangha—No interference—Petition dismissed. [Paras 39 to 45]

The concerned workmen were acquitted in the criminal case No. 01/2007 and therefore, they could not have been held to be guilty of the charges in the domestic enquiry, this Court is of the view that mere acquittal in a criminal case would not automatically absolve the workmen from the charges in the domestic enquiry. This Court has also noticed that the acquittal is on the benefit of doubt.

It was not proper to apply the analogy of a criminal case to a domestic enquiry. What is required in a domestic inquiry is that it should be held in accordance with the principles of natural justice and the delinquent should be given adequate opportunity of defence.
(iv) that all the workmen admitted the charges against them during the domestic enquiry :

Therefore, the High Court cannot entertain a petition for a writ of prohibition against the employer restraining him from proceeding with a domestic enquiry on the ground that some of the witnesses proposed to be examined were police officers who would be giving evidence against the workman in the criminal case in respect of the same matter.

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Sec. 10 (1)(c)—Domestic Enquiry—Held while delinquent workmen were in Jail custody—As they were arrested by Police—Nothing to show that they were arrested at instance of Management—No question of violation of Principles of Natural Justice arises when enquiry was conducted ex-parte thus.

Where the witnesses at the separate enquiries against separate workmen spoke against persons, who had no opportunity of cross-examining them, particularly, on the point of forming an unlawful assembly and such evidence was used against all the workmen without affording to each of them the opportunity of cross-examining the witnesses, held: This was a defect in the enquiry—violative, as it was, of principles of natural justice. That being so, the award of the Tribunal cannot be condemned on the ground that the tribunal sat as a court of appeal over the finding of the domestic enquiry and went beyond its jurisdiction.

Domestic enquiries are not enquiries in a court of law and ordinarily in these enquiries, simple questions of fact as to whether certain acts of misconduct were committed by a workman or not only fall to be considered. Straight forward questioning which a person of fair intelligence and knowledge of conditions prevailing in the establishment will be able to do will ordinarily help to elicit the truth. In most cases the accused workman will be best suited and fully able to cross-examine the witnesses who have spoken against him and to examine witnesses in his favour.

Dismissal for misconduct—Assault by workmen of Manager of factory alleged—Arrest of workmen and Criminal case—Finding by Criminal Court that case was concocted—Non-participation of workmen in Departmental enquiry Refusal of company to postpone enquiry till after decision of Criminal case—Victimisation for union activities alleged.

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Sec. 10—Indian Penal Code, 1860, Secs. 147, 341—Constitution of India, Art. 226—Workmen acquitted by Criminal Court on being given benefit of doubt—On same set of charges domestic enquiry conducted by employer—Whether domestic enquiry to proceed on such acquittals—Whether employer can adduce additional evidence before Labour Court to support its charges—Yes.

In a domestic inquiry held into alleged misconduct of a workman what is reasonable opportunity to be given to the workman depends on the facts of each case, depending particularly on the nature of the allegations, the witnesses and their availability and the time and assistance required for preparation to appear at the enquiry. Where the charge-sheet was given to the workman on February 20, 1975, to which he replied in time and he was informed only on April 2, 1975, that the enquiry would be held from April 3, 1975, and the nature of the allegations are such that only the workmen and the staff of the concern were possible witnesses and it did not require elaborate preparation of instructions and witnesses, it cannot be said that the workman was not given a fair opportunity in a case of assault, incitement and absenteeism confined to eye-witnesses of the concern itself. The basic right of a workman facing domestic enquiry is to cross-examine the employer’s witnesses in regard to the credibility and veracity of such witnesses and where there is no denial of this right, the finding of the Labour Court that the domestic enquiry was not defective cannot be said to be unjustified.

A criminal case was preferred against two workmen for assault of Manager of Factory. They were arrested. In the criminal case, they were acquitted on the finding that the case had been cooked up. In the departmental enquiry the workmen did not participate. They were found guilty and were dismissed. The workmen complain that the company was guilty of victimisation for their union activities, the principles of natural justice were violated and the company unjustifiably withheld payment of bonus for 1958-59.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Domestic enquiry started by employer against employee—Simultaneously criminal proceedings initiated by CBI on same charges—Principles of law—Employer should stay domestic enquiry pending final disposal of criminal case
Domestic enquiry—Stay of domestic enquiry pending disposal of criminal case—Desirability—Inference of mala fide where enquiry not stayed

Domestic enquiries—How to be conducted—Technical requirements of criminal law, if to be followed—Enquiry Officer claiming to have witnessed misconduct—Duty of.It is true that domestic enquiries need not be conducted in accordance with the technical requirements of criminal trials, but they must be fairly conducted and in holding them, considerations of fair play and natural justice must govern the conduct of the enquiry officer. Domestic enquiries must be conducted honestly and bona fide with a view to determine whether the charge framed against a particular employee is proved or not, and so, care must be taken to see that these enquiries do not become empty formalities. If an officer claims that he had himself seen the misconduct alleged against an employee, in fairness steps should be taken to see that the task of holding an enquiry is assigned to some other officer.Domestic enquiries—Duty of employer—Cross-examination of employee—Propriety.It is necessary to emphasise that in domestic enquiries, the employer should take steps first to lead evidence against the workman charged, give an opportunity to the workman to cross-examine the said evidence and then should the workman be asked whether he wants to give any explanation about the evidence led against him. It seems to us that it is not fair in domestic enquiries against industrial employees that at the very commencement of the enquiry, the employee should be closely cross-examined even before any other evidence is led against him. In dealing with domestic enquiries held in such industrial matters, we cannot overlook the fact that in a large majority of cases, employees are likely to be ignorant, and so, it is necessary not to expose them to the risk of cross-examination in the manner adopted in the enquiry proceedings in the instant case.Domestic enquiries—Date of—Intimation to workman—Opportunity, to prepare defence to be given.It may be that failure to intimate to the workman concerned about the date of the enquiry may, by itself, not constitute an infirmity in the enquiry, but, on the other hand, it is necessary to bear in mind that it would be fair if the workman is told as to when the enquiry is going to be held so that he has an opportunity to prepare himself to make his defence at the said enquiry and to collect such evidence as he may wish to lead in support of his defence. On the whole, it would not be right that the workman should be called on any day without previous intimation and the enquiry should begin straightaway. Such a course should ordinarily be avoided in holding domestic enquiries in industrial matters.

The company had two alternatives, either to act under standing order 47, or to take disciplinary action and hold a domestic enquiry. But the latter course would have meant that the company would have to launch into an enquiry almost parallel to the one which was going on before the committing magistrate.

Domestic enquiry—Nature of—Guilt of accused workman need not be established as in criminal prosecution—Proof of misconduct is sufficient—Strict rules of evidence not applicable—Complaint by person aggrieved by misconduct need not be in writing.

In a domestic enquiry a workman cannot claim as of right to be represented by counsel or an outsider [(1960) II L.L.J. 228] Where after the refusal by the management to be so represented the workmen withdrew from the enquiry, the enquiry officer preceded ex parte, examined a large number of witnesses and found the workman guilty of the charges, the enquiry cannot be held to be not full and fair, and the dismissal cannot be held to be unjustified. Hence approval of the action taken must be granted.

It may be that failure to intimate to the workman concerned about the date of the enquiry may, by itself, not constitute an infirmity in the enquiry, but, on the other hand, it is necessary to bear in mind that it would be fair if the workman is told as to when the enquiry is going to be held so that he has an opportunity to prepare himself to make his defence at the said enquiry and to collect such evidence as he may wish to lead in support of his defence. On the whole, it would not be right that the workman should be called on any day without previous intimation and the enquiry should begin straightaway. Such a course should ordinarily be avoided in holding domestic enquiries in industrial matters.

Held. The action of the company in not placing the full facts before the enquiry officer was not bona fide. The Company has not come with clean hands. Repeated requests by the workmen for postponement of the enquiry on the ground that it would otherwise prejudice the workman in the criminal case which was pending were not granted. The award is (i) reinstatement of the two workmen with continuity of service (2) full wages (3) payment of bonus for 1958-59.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal proceedings pending on same charges—Is no bar to domestic enquiry being held by employer—No right in employee to obtain temporary injunction against continuation of domestic enquiry.

In a domestic enquiry, the officer holding the enquiry can take no valid or effective steps to compel the attendance of any witness, just as the Company produced its witnesses before the officer, the concerned workman should have taken steps to produce his witnesses. It would be unreasonable to suggest that in a domestic enquiry, it is the right of the charge-sheeted employee to ask for as many adjournments as he likes. It is true that if it appears that by refusing to adjourn the hearing at the instance of the charge-sheeted workman the Enquiry Officer failed to give the said workman a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence that may in a proper case be considered to introduce an element of infirmity in the enquiry. But it was not possible to draw such an inference in the instant case. Hence it was held that the Tribunal was in error in coming to the conclusion that the enquiry suffered from the infirmity that it was conducted contrary to the principles of natural justice.

There are different standards of proof of the charges in the criminal case and domestic enquiry. Whereas in the criminal case charges must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, in the domestic enquiry the charges may be proved by preponderance of probabilities. Where the same witnesses are examined to prove the same charges both in the criminal Court and in the domestic enquiry, there should not be variance and contradictions in their statement.

The matter reached the Division Bench of the High Court on appeals by both the parties who felt aggrieved by the judgment of the single Judge. By a joint memo, both the parties requested the Appeal Court to decide the entire matter once for all on the basis of the material on record and grant appropriate relief finally in accordance with law, without’ remitting the matter to the Tribunal. The learned Judges agreed with the findings of the learned single Judge, that if anybody was to be blamed in this case it would be the workmen and their union for the stubborn and indifferent attitude in boycotting the enquiry and also held that the charge memo specified the acts of misconduct in sufficient particulars which clearly fell within standing order 26(5) and 26(12) and the acts of misconduct alleged against the workmen could not be said to be in any manner vague or jumbled up. However, they agreed with the finding recorded by the learned single Judge that the said report is not in accordance with law, since the Enquiry Officer did not consider the evidence of the witnesses as to the specific charges and he did not discuss the incriminating evidence against each worker in respect of each of the acts of misconduct alleged against him. After considering the evidence recorded ex parte in the domestic enquiry and the evidence recorded before the Tribunal on the preliminary issue, the learned Judges found the workmen guilty of wrongfully confining the President and compelling him to withdraw the notice issued by him but held that for these two acts of misconduct, the concerned workmen did not deserve the extreme penalty of dismissal and directed that they should be taken back on duty but with payment of one half of back wages.

In that case it was held that if the employer wanted to take disciplinary action on the ground that the employee was guilty of misconduct, it was absolutely essential that a proper enquiry should be held instead of equating the detention to a conviction by Criminal Court.

Misconduct—Domestic enquiry—Criminal case pending on same matter—Employer can decide whether to hold domestic enquiry or not—Employer cannot be prevented by writ of prohibition from proceeding with enquiry.

The petitioners have no legal right to insist that the enquiry proceedings against them are to be stayed till such time the Criminal Court concludes its trial. Possible prejudice to the interest of the employer also might have to be noticed, as it cannot be a one way traffic, and they are not expected to silently suffer in the bargain.

Domestic enquiry—Production of witnesses—Taking of steps—Duty of parties—Right of charge-sheeted workman to ask for adjournments—Failure of Enquiry Officer to give reasonable opportunity to lead evidence—Effect.

The fact that the worker was, after the domestic enquiry, acquitted by a criminal Court or even by criminal appellate Court would not in any way vitiate the finding arrived at by a domestic tribunal earlier on proper evidence and without violating any of the principles of natural justice.

Though normally it would be sufficient for a proper domestic enquiry that the delinquent had an opportunity of knowing what the charge was and opportunity to cross-examine such witnesses as were examined by the employer, where the facts disclose that other workmen and persons also had access to the place where an offence was alleged to have occurred but only the delinquent was searched on the basis of some information alleged to have been received by the security staff and certain concealed property was recovered, and it was possible that the property had been planted on the delinquent, the source of the information must be disclosed and the informant must be subjected to cross-examination by the delinquent. Otherwise, there will be victimisation of employees on foisted or cooked-up charges.

It is well settled that the approach and standard of proof in a criminal trial and in a domestic enquiry are different. The Labour Court considered the judgment of the Criminal Court but in the facts and circumstances of the case, decided not to give benefit of such acquittal to the workman. No fault can be found with the approach of the Labour Court.

It is well-settled that a domestic enquiry and a criminal trial can proceed simultaneously and the decision in the criminal case would not materially affect the outcome of the domestic enquiry. The nature of both the proceedings and the test applied to reach a final conclusion in the matter, are entirely different. The charge-memo dated 17.8.1987 records charges of grave indiscipline, misconduct, dereliction of duty and involvement in the criminal case. Obviously, the charges in the domestic enquiry and before the criminal Court were not similar.

The workman had been given the benefit of doubt and acquitted. As it was not a clean acquittal and also that the requirements and parameters of a criminal trial are vastly different with domestic enquiry, this cannot be a ground for upholding the award.

It is necessary to emphasise that in domestic enquiries, the employer should take steps first to lead evidence against the workman charged, give an opportunity to the workman to cross-examine the said evidence and then should the workman be asked whether he wants to give any explanation about the evidence led against him. It seems to us that it is not fair in domestic enquiries against industrial employees that at the very commencement of the enquiry, the employee should be closely cross-examined even before any other evidence is led against him. In dealing with domestic enquiries held in such industrial matters, we cannot overlook the fact that in a large majority of cases, employees are likely to be ignorant, and so, it is necessary not to expose them to the risk of cross-examination in the manner adopted in the enquiry proceedings in the instant case.

Five workmen were dismissed after a domestic enquiry. An industrial dispute was raised and the Labour Court found that the workmen were not given sufficient opportunity to establish their innocence and hence the enquiry to that extent was vitiated. Thereafter, additional evidence was taken and witnesses were examined for the workmen and the Labour Court found that the charges against the workmen were established and the workmen were discharged from service. On a writ petition challenging the order of the Labour Courtdischarging the services of the workmen, on the grounds that the employer should not have acted on evidence recorded at the domestic enquiry, that the findings of the employer were not supported by evidence, that since the domestic enquiry was illegal, all that took place during the enquiry was wiped out and that the punishment imposed was unduly harsh :

An enquiry, domestic or otherwise, into an act of misconduct by a workman is held in order to establish the guilt underlying the charge against him. While the employer conducts an enquiry to drive home the charge, the delinquent workman also has a right to lead evidence in support of his defence. Extenuating circumstances may lead the employer to take a lenient view if opportunity is not denied to lead such evidence as the workman may deem fit in support of his plea. If no such opportunity is given then any enquiry which proceeds on the basis that the explanation offered is prima facie confession of guilt would be vitiated by the rules of natural justice and fair play.

facts.text:
■

The dispute arose from an incident at Borjan Tea Estate in March 2007 when around 1,500 workers gathered at the factory gate; some forcefully entered, damaged office property, pelted stones, and the Manager sustained injuries, following which the Estate remained under lockout for 11 days. Eleven workmen were charge-sheeted for forming an unlawful assembly, instigating violence and damage to garden property, with alleged loss of about Rs. 19.66 lakhs, and were charged with gross misconduct under the Estate Standing Orders. The workmen denied involvement; the gateman stated the gate was broken by some workers after overpowering him. Separate domestic enquiries were conducted against each of the 11 workmen and enquiry reports held them guilty of gross misconduct. The management issued notices seeking representations; after time extension, no representations were submitted, and the workmen were dismissed from service, the Reference later describing dismissal as with effect from 10.09.2007.

■

Following the dismissal, the Government of Assam referred the dispute to the Labour Court, Dibrugarh, on whether the management was justified in dismissing the 11 named workmen and, if not, whether they were entitled to reinstatement with back wages. In its written statement, the management relied on the domestic enquiries as the basis for dismissal and reserved the right to adduce evidence on merits if the enquiries were found violative of natural justice. The workmen, in their written statement, asserted that the enquiries were not impartial, that they were denied opportunity to adduce defence evidence, and that the Presenting Officer for the management also acted as a witness; they denied instigating or participating in the violence.

■

The Labour Court proceeded to record evidence without first framing a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries. The proceedings initially went ex parte against the workmen; the management submitted evidence-in-chief and later stated it would not adduce further evidence. Management witnesses were cross-examined and the workmen also adduced evidence. The Enquiry Officer (examined as M.W. 4) stated in cross-examination that although workmen were informed of the enquiry and to participate, he did not inform them that they were required to adduce evidence, stating that the Presenting Officer would inform them. The records of the domestic enquiries were not placed before the Labour Court. The Head Clerk (examined as M.W. 2), whose evidence had formed the basis of the domestic findings, admitted in cross-examination that he did not remember the names of the workers involved in the incident. The enquiry reports recorded that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and did not give reasons for proceeding only against these 11 workmen.

■

By Award dated 29.02.2016 in Reference Case No. 02/2009, the Labour Court upheld the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries and, on that basis, upheld the dismissal of the workmen; no separate finding on proportionality of the punishment was recorded.

■

On writ petition to the High Court.

■

A dispute arose between the appellant–Management and its workmen following a strike. The Management issued a show cause notice on 11-5-2011, placed the workmen under suspension, and issued charge memoranda. A domestic enquiry was conducted in which the workmen participated. The Enquiry Officer held the charges proved, following which a second show cause notice dated 17-8-2011 was issued. The explanations submitted by the workmen were rejected and orders of removal from service were passed on 20-8-2011. Aggrieved thereby, the workmen raised industrial disputes in I.D. Nos. 33, 34, 35, 36 and 37 of 2011 before the Labour Court, Pondicherry.

■

Before the Labour Court, the Management, in its written statement, specifically reserved its right to adduce additional evidence in the event the domestic enquiry was held to be unfair or defective. The parties adduced oral and documentary evidence. However, the Labour Court did not decide the fairness of the domestic enquiry as a preliminary issue; instead, while passing the final award, it held that the enquiry was not conducted in a free and fair manner and ordered reinstatement of the workmen.

■

The Management challenged the awards in writ petitions under article 226, but the writ Court confirmed the Labour Court’s awards.

■

Aggrieved thereby, the Management preferred intra-Court appeals before the High Court.

The Central Excise authorities imposed penalty and demanded duty from the appellants on the ground that the since the latter employed six or more workers in their factory they were not entitled to the benefits under No fn. No. 90/76 dated 16.3.1976 and had therefore to take out the necessary licence and remove the goods after payment of excise duty which they railed to do. The appellants contended that there were only five workers employed and not more. They also contended that since they had been acquitted of the same charge by the Criminal Court the Tribunal was bound by that judgment. They finally contended that as the matter of duty liability was under consideration by the Asstt. Collector there could be no case of wilful infraction of any of the statutory provisions and there was, therefore, no need for imposition of a penalty.

■

The petitioner–company engaged respondent No.1 as an underground loader. The company alleged that he remained absent from duty without authorization from December 1997, issued a charge sheet for misconduct, received his reply, and conducted a domestic enquiry in which the workman participated. The Enquiry Officer held the charges proved. After issuing a show-cause notice and considering the workman’s explanation along with the enquiry record, the Enquiry Officer’s report, and the past service record, the disciplinary authority dismissed the workman from service for misconduct.

■

Respondent No.2–union raised an industrial dispute on behalf of the workman. Conciliation failed, and the Government of India referred the dispute to the Central Government Industrial Tribunal on the question whether the dismissal was legal and justified, and the relief, if any, to the workman.

■

Before the Tribunal, an initial order held the domestic enquiry valid and fair. The parties filed documents; a medical certificate produced by the workman, not part of the domestic enquiry record, was admitted in evidence. In its final award, the Tribunal recorded that the workman had medical treatment and a certificate, found that he was not afforded fair opportunity in the domestic enquiry, held the enquiry devoid of fairness and propriety, declared the dismissal not legal or justified, directed reinstatement with back wages from the date of dismissal, excluded wages for the period of pre-disciplinary absence if not covered by leave, imposed a 25% cut in pendent lite wages, and directed disbursement of monetary benefits within a time frame.

■

On the petitioner’s writ to the High Court.

Demand notices were served on the appellants for duty payable on cotton fabrics manufactured on powerlooms since the Assistant Collector was of the view that the appellants were not entitled to exemption granted only to units which manufactured cotton fabrics on less than five powerlooms. He held that the appellants were the actual manufacturers of the fabrics said to have been manufactured through various other weaving mills and that the firm from which the yarn was supplied was fictitious and merely a camouflage set up by the appellants. The Collr., however, held that there had been no proper investigation in the absence of statements recorded from partners in the firm and that there was violation of the principles of natural justice.

■

The respondent–workman, employed in a defence organisation (Gun Carriage Factory, Jabalpur), was charged with stealing brass and copper pieces. A departmental inquiry was initiated. On different dates the respondent did not appear; when he appeared, he admitted the charges, and on subsequent dates he again remained absent. The inquiry officer submitted a report holding him guilty. After issuing notice, the disciplinary authority imposed the penalty of removal from service.

■

The CGIT held that the termination was not proper and legal, quashed the penalty of removal, and awarded compensation of Rs. 2.5 lakhs to the respondent.

■

In the employer’s writ, the High Court upheld the quashing of the removal order but gave liberty to proceed with the inquiry from the stage of express denial of charges, directed that reasonable opportunity be afforded to engage a defence assistant, and that the inquiry be conducted under Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965. The High Court quashed the compensation, deemed the workman to be under suspension till conclusion of the inquiry, and directed that the inquiry be concluded expeditiously and preferably within six months.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the employer contended that the charges concerned theft in a defence factory; the respondent repeatedly remained absent; he had admitted the charges; the inquiry officer found him guilty; the disciplinary authority, after notice, removed him; and the CGIT exceeded its limited scope of interference, with compensation being unwarranted. The respondent contended he was coerced to accept the charges and that lack of a defence assistant led to miscarriage of justice.

■

The petitioner–workman was dismissed by the respondent–employer (I.T.C., Munger) pursuant to a domestic enquiry. The industrial dispute regarding the dismissal was referred to the Labour Court, Bhagalpur as Reference Case No. 01 of 1992.

■

During the reference, the Labour Court by order dated 26.07.1999 held the domestic enquiry fair and proper and then fixed the case for evidence to produce and exhibit the documents and materials that were part of the domestic enquiry for appraisal. By award dated 28.12.2012, the Labour Court upheld the dismissal as just and proper and denied any relief to the workman.

■

Before the High Court, the petitioner contended that under the proviso to Section 11A the Labour Court was barred from taking fresh evidence and that fixing the case for evidence violated the proviso; the respondent submitted that no fresh evidence was taken and only materials from the domestic enquiry were exhibited for reappraisal. The High Court called for and examined the lower court records.

■

The petitioner was engaged in the business of manufacturing compact fin heat exchangers, plate heat exchangers, single tube heat exchangers, transformer cooling system etc. and also provided solutions to various industries, including transportation, energy, oil, gas etc. The respondents were working with the petitioner in various positions as workmen.

■

It was alleged that on 19-2-2020, office bearers of a union called upon the workmen to gather at the gate of the factory. Instead of starting the work and performing normal duties, the workmen gathered in front of the gate of the factory. The Managing Director of the company attempted to pacify the union leaders, as well as the entire mob of the workmen and repeatedly requested them not to resort to any indiscipline and to commence the work. However, the mob of the workmen refused to act on the request of the Managing Director and later became violent. It was alleged that the mob broke glasses, threw stones on the bus and security cabin. The company was left with no option but to call the police. The crowd went on rampage till arrival of the police. The police disbursed the mob and arrested the union leader and few others.

■

It was alleged that since 20-2-2020, the respondent-workmen did not report for work. It was alleged that the acts committed by the respondent-workmen amounted to illegal strike causing unprecedented damage and loss to the company. It was alleged that the respondent workmen committed serious misconduct under Clauses 24(a), 24(b), 24(k) and 24(l) of the Model Standing Orders.

■

The respondent-workmen submitted their respective replies to the chargesheets. The supplementary chargesheet was issued alleging unauthorised absence from 20-2-2020 and misconduct under Clause 24(f) of the Model standing orders. By the supplementary chargesheet, a practising advocate was also appointed as Enquiry Officer.

■

The Enquiry Officer conducted enquiry and submitted report holding that misconduct under Clauses 24(a), (k), (l) and (f) was fully proved. The misconduct alleged under Clause 24(b) was held to be disproved.

■

The petitioner passed orders dismissing the respondent-employees from service based on the findings of the Enquiry Officer. At the instance of the respondents, References were made by the appropriate Government to Labour Court relating to termination of services of the respondent-workmen under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

■

The respondent-workmen filed their Statements of Claim, which were resisted by filing Written Statements by the petitioner-employer. The Labour Court proceeded to frame preliminary issues relating to fairness in the enquiry and perversity in the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer.

■

The Labour Court held that departmental enquiry conducted against the respondent-workmen is legal, fair and proper. However, it held that the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer to the extent of charges under Clauses (a), (k), (l) and (f) of MSO, 2024 are perverse.

■

On appeal:

■

Three members of the petitioner-Union were dismissed from service. The Management invoked section 33(2)(b) seeking approval for a penalty of dismissal. ■

The workman, a driver employed with the respondent–transport corporation, was issued a charge memo alleging rash and negligent driving causing injury to a pedestrian. He explained that the pedestrian suddenly turned after being called from the opposite side, lost balance, fell, and sustained injuries. The injured pedestrian filed a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.

■

In the domestic enquiry, the driver was found guilty. After a second show cause notice, punishment of postponement of increment for two years with cumulative effect was imposed, and the suspension period was treated as eligible leave. The trade union challenged the punishment in I.D. No. 63 of 2023.

■

In the MACT proceedings (M.C.O.P. No. 353 of 2018), the transport corporation filed a counter replicating the driver’s explanation and specifically stating that the driver was not negligent and not responsible for the accident. While the management referred to the MACT case in its counter in the industrial dispute, it did not produce a copy of the MACT counter before the Labour Court.

■

The Labour Court, on consideration of documents from both sides, recorded that the enquiry was fair and confirmed the punishment imposed by the management. A writ petition was filed challenging the Labour Court’s award.

■

On appeal to the High Court, the petitioner contended that the management had accepted the driver’s explanation and reiterated it in the MACT counter but suppressed that pleading before the Labour Court, relying on a Supreme Court decision against taking contradictory stands. The respondent–transport corporation contended that the driver should have been more careful in a busy locality, that the accident led to financial loss by way of compensation, and that its MACT counter could not be relied upon in the domestic enquiry and it was entitled to defend the MACT claim independently.

■

The petitioner–management of Gopinath Colliery under Eastern Coalfields Ltd. dismissed the concerned workman on 24/25-6-1982 after a domestic enquiry conducted pursuant to a charge-sheet dated 11-3-1981 alleging distortion and manipulation of wage figures, payment of lesser wages than actually billed to certain workers, and failure to record wage payments in identity cards.

■

After about 15 years, the workman challenged the dismissal before the Calcutta High Court by filing W.P. No. 22533 of 1997. The writ petition was dismissed on 20-2-1998 on the ground of delay and laches. The intra-court appeal was also dismissed on 24-2-1999 on account of delay of 254 days and other defects. Thereafter, on 19-9-2001, the Central Government referred the dispute under section 10(1)(d) read with section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to the Central Government Industrial Tribunal No. I, Dhanbad for adjudication of the validity of the dismissal and the relief, if any. By then, about 19 years had elapsed from the date of dismissal.

■

Before the Tribunal, both parties filed written statements and the management specifically pleaded that the reference was belated and the dispute had become stale. The Tribunal had earlier, by order dated 31-8-2006, held the domestic enquiry to be unfair and granted opportunity to the management to adduce evidence. By award dated 28-1-2009, the Tribunal rejected the plea of delay on the ground that the Industrial Disputes Act prescribed no limitation period, held the dismissal unfair and unjustified, and directed reinstatement of the workman with full back wages and consequential benefits within 30 days of publication of the award.

■

Aggrieved by the award dated 28-1-2009 passed in Reference No. 32 of 2002, the management filed the present writ petition before the High Court.

■

The respondent–workman was charge-sheeted for alleged theft of cables manufactured by the appellant–management. An Enquiry Officer and a Presenting Officer were appointed. The workman requested permission to engage a lawyer in view of the Presenting Officer’s experience and bio-data; the request was denied. The enquiry proceeded with the workman represented by a union leader; management witnesses were cross-examined at length, and the workman re-examined himself. The Enquiry Officer submitted a report, and the disciplinary authority dismissed the workman.

■

Before the Tribunal under Section 2A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the management’s objection to the applicability of Section 2A(2) was rejected; after considering Supreme Court decisions, the Tribunal held that the workman suffered prejudice from denial of legal representation and passed an interim award.

■

In a writ petition, the management challenged the interim award and also assailed the constitutional vires of Section 2A(2). The Single Bench dismissed the vires challenge and, on review, upheld the Tribunal’s observations that the workman suffered prejudice from denial of a lawyer.

■

On intra-court appeal before the High Court, the record showed that the workman had extensively cross-examined management witnesses and re-examined himself during the enquiry.

The petitioners, against whom criminal proceedings were pending, were issued a show cause notice by the customs authorities as to why action should not be taken against them under the Customs Act in regard to violation of the provisions of the Act by them. The petitioners urged that as criminal proceedings on identical facts and circumstances were being taken against them, the proceedings should be stayed as their statements as witnesses may be incriminating, and that calling on them to disclose their defence prematurely would be testimonial compulsion, violating the guarantee under Article 20(3) of the Constitution.

■

The workman was issued a charge memo on 07.05.2014 and, after a domestic enquiry, was dismissed from service on 09.08.2014. He challenged the dismissal under Section 2A(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Labour Court held the enquiry was not fair and in accordance with natural justice, permitted the management to lead fresh evidence (Exhibits M1 to M14 and one witness), and after evaluating the evidence found the enquiry report perverse, held that the charges were not proved, set aside the dismissal, and directed reinstatement. The management did not challenge the award of reinstatement.

■

After ordering reinstatement, the Labour Court rejected the workman’s claim for back wages on the ground that he had not come forward to attend duty or approached the management for re-employment, observing that back wages on reinstatement are not automatic but depend on the facts and circumstances.

■

On writ petition before the High Court, the workman challenged the denial of back wages, contending that once dismissed and while contesting the dismissal he could not be expected to approach the management for re-employment, and pointing out that in paragraph 8 of his claim petition he had pleaded suffering due to non-employment from the date of dismissal, which was not specifically disputed by the management before the Labour Court. The management contended that the workman had not established that he was not gainfully employed during the period of non-employment.

The petitioner was in employment of OP No. 2-company and while he was in service, he was extended the facility of residential accommodation. Subsequently, the petitioner’s service was terminated and the company asked him to vacate the residential quarter. In spite of notice and reminders, the petitioner did not vacate the premises and, therefore, he was alleged to have committed offence under section 630. The petitioner, by filing the instant petition, prayed for quashing the entire criminal proceedings initiated against him alleging that the termination of his service was illegal and the Government had referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication and, thus, under such circumstances, criminal proceedings under section 630 could not be initiated against him.

■

The petitioner, an employee of the respondent–power distribution company, was issued a show-cause notice after registration of a corruption offence alleging demand of Rs. 3,000. He denied the allegations. No departmental enquiry was initiated or conducted, and he was dismissed from service solely on the ground of registration of the offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act. He filed Complaint (ULP) No. 50 of 2014 before the Labour Court.

■

The respondents filed their written statement before the Labour Court. On perusal of the record, there were no averments explaining impracticability of holding an enquiry and no express reservation in the written statement seeking permission to lead evidence before the Court to prove misconduct.

■

The respondents filed Revision (ULP) No. 59 of 2017. The Industrial Court allowed the revision, set aside the Labour Court’s order dated 05.01.2017 in Complaint (ULP) No. 50 of 2014, and remanded the matter with a direction to frame an additional issue on whether the respondents proved the alleged charges of misconduct before the Court.

■

On writ petition before the High Court.

■

The respondent-workman, employed as a driver with the petitioner-Corporation since 1986, was alleged to have remained absent without authorization from 12.02.1995 to 15.07.1995. Articles of charge were issued, and his services were terminated by order dated 27.10.1995.

■

The workman initiated proceedings under Section 10(4-A) of the I.D. Act in KID No.39/2001, which were dismissed by award dated 06.03.2003. He thereafter sought conciliation; the Government refused by order dated 17.05.2005. In W.P.No.24390/2005, this Court on 20.01.2006 quashed the Government's refusal and remanded for reconsideration. Consequent thereto, the Government made a reference under Section 10(1)(C)(D) in Reference No.3/2007.

■

In the reference proceeding, the Labour Court framed issues on the fairness of the domestic enquiry, the justification of dismissal, and relief. It held the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper as the Corporation did not produce enquiry records; on delay it recorded, with reference to this Court's earlier order, that the dispute was subsisting and the delay was not fatal; and on merits, after appreciating the charge sheet, dismissal order and correspondence, it held the Corporation failed to prove misconduct, noting that both sides admitted about five months' absence and that the workman cited his and his wife's illness (she later died) and a leave application, which the Corporation disputed.

■

By award dated 07.11.2008, the Labour Court set aside the removal order dated 27.10.1995, directed reinstatement with continuity of service and consequential benefits, denied back wages, and directed that the period from 27.10.1995 till the date of the award be treated as leave without pay.

■

On the Corporation's writ petition to the High Court.

The complainant-company had allotted staff quarters to the respondents for residential purpose during their employment with the complainant. Services of the respondents were terminated by the complainant and, consequently, the respondents were required to hand over quarters to the complainant, but they did not do so, despite notice for vacating the same. The complainant lodged complaint under section 630. The trial court, after appreciating the evidence on record, convicted the respondents under section 630.

On appeal of the respondents, the Sessions Court reversed the finding of the trial court on the ground that as the labour proceedings challenging the termination of the respondents by the complainant were pending in the competent Labour Court, the termination itself could not be said to be legal and, therefore, withholding of the quarters could not be said to be wrongful.

■

The workman was engaged as a peon with the management–bank, claimed from 10.09.2003, and stated he worked continuously until 06.02.2006 when he was removed on an allegation of theft. The management subsequently issued a letter dated 16.02.2006 alleging theft from the strong room. The workman’s demand notice went unanswered; conciliation failed; the dispute was referred for adjudication.

■

In the industrial adjudication, the management’s witness (MW-1) admitted the workman’s engagement as a peon from 10.09.2003 and the existence of an attendance register, which was not produced despite opportunities. The workman produced salary receipt vouchers (Ex.WW1/12 to Ex.WW1/18) evidencing continuity. MW-1 had joined the office on 16.02.2006 and could not attest the alleged theft; he conceded no notice, notice pay, or service compensation was given. The show cause notice on theft was issued on 16.02.2006, i.e., after the 06.02.2006 removal; no domestic enquiry was conducted. The alleged confessional letter (Ex.WW1/M1) was not proved as neither the addressee Bank Manager nor the attesting witness was examined; and the assertion of resignation on 06.02.2006 was inconsistent with the subsequent 16.02.2006 show cause. The Labour Court held the termination illegal for violation of Section 25-F and, in lieu of reinstatement, directed monetary compensation of Rs. 1 lakh with interest at 9% per annum from the date of publication of the award.

■

On writ petitions before the High Court.

■

The complaint was instituted by the Assistant Director of Factories and Boilers, Cuttack Zone-II, arising out of an accident inside a registered factory where an unloading helper engaged in unloading hard coke was hit by a truck on 04.05.2018 and later died on 05.05.2018. The Management telephonically informed the authority on 04.05.2018 and submitted the statutory accident report in Form No.18 on 05.05.2018.

■

The complaint was filed on 02.08.2018 before the S.D.J.M., Athgarh. On 25.08.2018, the court took cognizance under Section 92 of the Factories Act.

■

The petitioner-accused had invoked the jurisdiction of this Court under section 482 of the Cr.P.C. seeking quashing of the entire criminal prosecution launched against him and also challenged the order dated 25-8-2018 passed by SDJM.

Cotton fabrics processed without the aid of power or steam and those not subjected to the process of bleaching, dyeing or printing with the aid of machines were exempted from duty under Notfn. No. 130/82, which, the appellant contended, applied to processed/dyed fabrics manufactured by them as the hand driven jiggers used in the factory were worked by manual labour and were not machines. They contended that such a simple appliance could not be termed a machine, and also objected to the imposition of penalty as there was no mala fide intention to evade duty on their part.

The petitioner-Association made a representation to the Collector of Central Excise, Combater, to grant exemption to its members from payment of excise duty on cone yarn wound on their cone winding machines. The contention was that the processes of manufacture enumerated in S. 2(f)(iv) of the CE S. Act applied only to grey cotton yarn, not to dyed cotton yarn in loose form, which was being used by the members for winding, and that inclusion of cones in Item 18 was ultra vires.

Waste cotton yarn in tangled form produced by the appellants was assessed in the RT 12 returns for cotton yarn by the excise authorities on the basis of duty leviable on the highest count manufactured by their mills. A Show Cause Notice, demanding duty was issued subsequently, but the appellants protested that the notice did not result in a proper adjudication and that the original assessment in the RT 12 was in violation of the principles of natural justice as no opportunity for a hearing was provided. Contending that they had claimed exemption for waste cotton yarn under Notfn. No. 95/61, they pointed out that the stage at which the waste cotton yarn should result so as to be eligible for exemption was not specified by the notification. Also, the count of the yarn cleared was well below the highest count.

held.text:
■

The narration of facts herein above and a perusal of the impugned Award would show that the learned Labour Court did not specifically frame a preliminary issue as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries which were held against the workmen. It is apposite out here to mention that at paragraph Nos. 5, 6, and 7 as well as at paragraph No. 14 of the written statement filed by the management, the reports of the domestic enquiries were relied upon by the management to justify their stand for dismissing the workmen. Under such circumstances, it was the requirement of law that the learned Labour Court ought to have framed a preliminary issue on the legality and validity of the domestic enquiries held against the workmen. [Para 22]

■

This Court also finds it pertinent to observe that a perusal of the impugned Award shows that though no preliminary issue was framed regarding the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports, but what was decided in the impugned Award was only the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports. The learned Labour Court further did not proceed to decide anything else. [Para 23]

■

It surprises this Court to take note of that the learned Labour Court while passing the impugned Award, after upholding the domestic enquiries held against the workmen, did not decide as regards the proportionality of the punishments which have been imposed against the workmen, which was a jurisdiction conferred upon the learned Labour Court to decide. The procedure therefore followed by the learned Labour Court, in the opinion of this Court amounts to a jurisdictional error committed by the learned Labour Court. [Para 24]

■

This Court finds it very pertinent to take note of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of M.L. Singla v. Punjab National Bank [2019] 9 taxmann.com 1153 (SC)/(2018) 18 SCC 21, wherein the Supreme Court observed the procedure to be followed when a domestic enquiry is being relied upon. [Para 25]

■

The proposition of law as laid down by the Supreme Court in M.L. Singla (supra) clearly show that when a domestic enquiry is being relied upon, it is the requirement of law that the preliminary issue be framed as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry report and thereupon, if it is held that the domestic enquiry report is in order, then to decide as to whether the imposition of punishment was proportionate. In the instant case, it would be seen that the learned Labour Court vide the impugned Award only decided as regards the legality and validity of the domestic enquiry reports and held it to be fair and thereupon upheld the termination of the workmen. [Para 26]

■

Taking into account the submissions so made by the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, this Court finds it pertinent to look into, as to whether, the opinion rendered by the learned Labour Court holding the domestic enquiries to be fair is in consonance with the well-settled principles of law. [Para 27]

■

From a perusal of the materials on record, and more particularly, the evidence adduced by the management witness No.4 before the learned Labour Court, who was the Enquiry Officer, he during his cross-examination, categorically mentioned that though information was provided to the workmen as regards the appointment of an Enquiry Officer and to participate in the domestic enquiry proceedings, but he did not inform the workmen that they are required to adduce evidence. In fact, during his cross-examination, he mentioned that the Presenting Officer would be informing the workmen that they would be required to adduce evidence. [Para 28]

■

This Court also finds it very surprising to take note of that without the records of the domestic enquiries being placed before the learned Labour Court as to how the evidence was adduced and as to whether the observers were present inasmuch as such evidence would be available in the Minutes recorded during the course of the domestic enquiries. [Para 29]

■

■

Admittedly, the petitioner has not obtained prior permission under Section 25M of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 before the layoff was effected. The justification put forth by the petitioner is that, the lay-off was occasioned by the COVID-19 pandemic, which according to the petitioner is a "natural calamity", under Section 25M and the prior permission is not required. [Para 10]

■

Whether the COVID-19 pandemic would fall within the scope of "natural calamity" under Section 25M or the lay-off is otherwise justified without there being a prior permission, are matters which are presently pending adjudication before the Tribunal/Labour Court under Section 10. This Court does not propose to examine the said issue in this petition. [Para 11]

■

The petitioner's contention that criminal prosecution cannot be initiated under Section 34 pending adjudication of the dispute under Section 10, where the allegations in both proceedings are one and the same cannot be accepted in absolute terms. In appropriate cases, there can be simultaneous proceedings under Sections 10 and 34. In some cases, the simultaneous proceedings may not be desirable. [Para 13]

■

While considering such a question on permissibility of simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication proceeding, in the context of two different enactments, the Apex Court in P. Jayappan v. S.K. Perumal, First ITO ([1984] 19 Taxman 1 (SC) /1984 (Supp) SCC 437), and Radheshyam Kejriwal v. State of West Bengal ([2011] 12 taxmann.com 107/108 SCL 406 (SC)/(2011) 3 SCC 581) has held that such criminal prosecution pending adjudication of dispute is permissible. On behalf of the respondent-Union, these two judgments are cited to justify the simultaneous application under Sections 10 and 34. [Para 14]

■

In P. Jayappan (supra), the Apex Court was considering Section 276-C of Income Tax Act, 1961 (Act, 1961) and in Radheshyam Kejriwal (supra), Section 56 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (Act, 1973). In both the enactments, the provisions of law provide for simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of a claim or liability under the said Acts. [Para 15]

■

Section 276-C of Act, 1961 which provides for criminal prosecution, uses the expression "without prejudice to any penalty that may be imposable on him under any other provisions of this Act". Likewise, Section 56 of the Act, 1973, uses the expression "Without prejudice to any award of penalty by the adjudicating officer under this Act". [Para 16]

■

From the language employed in the aforementioned two provisions, it is explicit that, the simultaneous criminal prosecution for the violation of the provisions of the aforementioned two Acts, even before the adjudication takes place on the claim or liability under the respective Acts, is expressly provided. [Para 17]

■

In the Act there is no provision which uses similar expression which expressly provides for simultaneous criminal prosecution and adjudication of a claim or liability under the Act. Thus, in a way it is possible to urge a contention that, the simultaneous prosecution pending adjudication of the dispute alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is not permissible. [Para 18]

■

At the same time, one has to notice that there is no provision which specifically bars simultaneous criminal prosecution pending adjudication of any claim or liability by any other authority/Tribunal/Court under the Act. [Para 19]

■

To answer the questions raised, the Court has to keep in mind the object of the Act. One of the objects is to provide efficacious remedy to the workmen against the violations of the provisions of the Act. At the same time, among other, the Act also aims in securing industrial peace. [Para 20]

■

If these two aspects are borne in mind, it is not permissible to accept the contention that the complaint under Section 34 alleging violation of the provisions of the Act is permissible only in a situation where the adjudication gets concluded by the authority/Court/Tribunal relating to the violation of the provisions of the Act. [Para 21]

■

At the same time it is not possible to accept the contention that every application alleging violation of the provisions of the Act, seeking permission to prosecute for alleged violation of the provisions of the Act, will have to be allowed pending adjudication of the dispute arising from such violations of the provisions of the Act. [Para 22]

■

Yarn manufactured and consumed captively for manufacture of fabrics in an integrated process is liable to duty on the basis of the weight of the yarn at the spindle stage and not on the basis of weight of sized yarn (ratio of Supreme Court judgment in JK Cotton Spinning Weaving Mills Ltd. Anr. v. UOI Ors.). Show cause notices quashed. "These petitions were admitted to hearing in view of the pendency of the........appeal in the case of J.K. Cotton Mills and in view of the decision of the Delhi High Court which was appealed against in the aforesaid case of J.K. Cotton Mills. Practically nine years have gone by now and the impugned show cause notices have been issued by virtue of the same directives which were subject matter of the aforesaid case of J.K. Cotton Mills. In view of this peculiar fact it would not be in the interest of justice if the parties are directed to contest the individual show cause notices issued by the respondents in view of the aforesaid directives. In order to avoid multiplicity of proceedings involving time and expense, we quash the impugned notices in all the cases.........The result is that alt the aforesaid writ petitions are accepted and the impugned show cause notices are quashed."
