Comments

Case Laws

Jurisdiction Barred by Existing Industrial Award - The dispute arose when an employee of Bombay Gas Company filed an application under section 15(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, claiming overtime wages under section 59 of the Factories Act. The employer contended that the claim was barred by an existing Industrial Tribunal award from 1953, which had settled the issue of overtime compensation for meter readers and their assistants. That award, based on a concession that these employees were not covered by the Factories Act, allowed only limited extra wages and was still in force at the time of the application. The Supreme Court held that the Authority under the Payment of Wages Act had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. So long as the 1953 award remained in force and unmodified under section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, employees could not invoke section 15(2) to claim contrary benefits. Allowing such a claim would effectively permit the Authority to sit in appeal over the Tribunal's award, which it cannot do. The appeal was allowed and the employee's application was dismissed - Bombay Gas Co. Ltd. v. Shridhar Bhau Parab AIR 1961 SUPREME COURT 1196.

Termination of Service - Employer's Action not Abandonment by Employees - Employees of Express Newspapers Ltd. in Bombay went on strike on December 31, 1956, after the employer failed to meet certain demands. The management issued notices warning that failure to resume work would be treated as abandonment, and ultimately removed the strikers' names from the muster rolls on January 14, 1957. A number of workmen, including the respondents, filed applications under section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, claiming wages in lieu of notice and other dues under Standing Order No. 25, which provided compensation upon termination by the employer. The Supreme Court held that the workers had not abandoned their employment by striking to press demands, and their conduct could not be equated with voluntary desertion. The employer could have taken disciplinary action for the strike if it was illegal, but instead, it unilaterally declared abandonment without following any disciplinary process. The removal of names from the muster roll amounted to termination of service without notice. Hence, the workers were entitled to compensation under Standing Order 25, enforceable through section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act. The appeals by the employer were dismissed - Express Newspapers Private Ltd. v. Michael Mark AIR 1963 SUPREME COURT 1141.

Act not to apply to certain industrial establishments

13B. Nothing in this Act shall apply to an industrial establishment insofar as the workmen employed therein are persons to whom the Fundamental and Supplementary Rules, Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, Civil Services (Temporary Services) Rules, Revised Leave Rules, Civil Service Regulations, Civilians in Defence Service (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules or the Indian Railway Establishment Code or any other rules or regulations that may be notified in this behalf by the appropriate Government in the Official Gazette, apply.]

COMMENTS

CASE LAWS

Regulations can supersede certified Standing Orders via single notification - The petitioner, an employee of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, challenged disciplinary proceedings initiated against him under the Corporation's Conduct and Discipline Regulations, 1971, arguing that certified standing orders made under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act were still in force and that no separate notification under section 13B had been issued to exclude their applicability. The Karnataka High Court rejected this contention, holding that a single notification issued under section 45 of the Road Transport Corporations Act, 1950, granting previous sanction to the Regulations, was sufficient to also serve as notification under section 13B of the Standing Orders Act. The Court emphasized that Regulation 39 explicitly repealed the earlier certified standing orders regarding conduct and discipline, and that the State Government must have been aware of this when granting approval. Thus, the certified standing orders stood repealed by implication, and the 1971 Regulations validly governed disciplinary matters. The Court further held that even if the Regulations were less favourable, they remained enforceable and the petitioner could not challenge them on that basis - K. V. R. Shetty v. The Secretary to Government, Home Department, Govt. of Karnataka 1980 LAB. I. C. 194.

302. (1) Whenever, in the course of an inquiry, trial or proceeding under this Sanhita, it appears to a Criminal Court,—

(a)

that a person confined or detained in a prison should be brought before the Court for answering to a charge of an offence, or for the purpose of any proceedings against him; or

the Court may make an order requiring the officer in charge of the prison to produce such person before the Court answering to the charge or for the purpose of such proceeding or for giving evidence.

(2) Where an order under sub-section (1) is made by a Magistrate of the second class, it shall not be forwarded to, or acted upon by, the officer in charge of the prison unless it is countersigned by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, to whom such Magistrate is subordinate.

Application of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947

.

39. (1) The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) shall apply to matters arising in respect of every industrial premises.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a dispute between an employer and employee relating to—

(a)

the issue by the employer of raw materials to the employees;

(b)

the rejection by the employer of beedi or cigar or both made by an employee;

(c)

the payment of wages for the beedi or cigar or both rejected by the employer,

11[shall be referred for settlement within such time and by such authority as the State Government may, by rules, specify in this behalf and such rules may also provide for the summary manner in which such dispute shall be settled.]

(3) Any person aggrieved by a settlement made by the authority specified under sub-section (2) may prefer an appeal to such authority and within such time as the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify in this behalf.

(4) The decision of the authority specified under sub-section (3) shall be final.

COMMENTS

CASE LAWS

Application of Industrial Disputes Act to home workers – The Bombay High Court held that the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966, does not exclude the application of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to establishments beyond industrial premises, such as private dwelling houses where home workers are employed. The Court emphasized that while section 39(1) applies the Industrial Disputes Act to industrial premises, it does not bar its application to other establishments covered under the Beedi Act. It clarified that home workers, considered employees under section 2(f) of the Beedi Act, can claim laid-off compensation and other rights under section 25C of the Industrial Disputes Act, filling gaps in the Beedi Act's provisions. – Abdul Sattar Rehmanbhai Musa Beedi v. Smt. Julekha Bi Rahiman Daryawardi 1988 LAB IC 714.

Jurisdiction over bonus disputes in beedi factories – The Allahabad High Court held that section 39(1) of the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966, does not preclude the application of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, or related proceedings under the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, concerning disputes over bonus payments in beedi factories. It emphasized that while the Beedi Act governs conditions of employment, the Bonus Act addresses bonus entitlement—a distinct aspect of service conditions. The Court clarified that disputes related to bonus payments are validly referable under the Industrial Disputes Act, reinforcing that overlapping legislation operates within separate domains. – Kale Khan Mohd. Hanif v. Jhansi Biri Mazdoor Union 1980 LAB IC 1073.

Applicability of Industrial Disputes Act – The Patna High Court clarified that section 39 of the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966, does not exclude the application of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to workers employed in industrial premises governed by the Beedi Act. While section 39(1) retains the machinery for industrial adjudication under the Industrial Disputes Act, section 39(2) provides additional safeguards for specific disputes, such as rejection of products or wage disputes, to be settled by a designated authority under the Beedi Act. This dual mechanism ensures comprehensive protection of workers' rights. – Management of M/s. Belal Biri Factory (P) Ltd. v. Union of India 1978 LAB IC 1493.

Manner of holding enquiry

53. (1) Where a complaint is filed before the officer appointed under sub-section (1) of section 53 (hereinafter in this rule referred to as "the officer") in respect of the offences referred to in said sub-section, either by an officer authorised for such purpose by the Central Government or by an employee aggrieved or a registered trade union registered under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (35 of 2020) or an Inspector-cum-Facilitator, the officer after considering such evidence as produced by the complainant, is of the opinion that an offence has been committed, shall issue summons to the offender on the address specified in the complaint fixing a date for his appearance.

(2) If the offender to whom the summons has been issued under sub-rule (1) appears or is produced before the officer, the officer shall explain the offender the offence complained against and if the offender pleads guilty, the officer shall impose penalty in accordance with the provisions of the Code and if the offender does not plead guilty, the officer shall take evidence of the witnesses produced by the complainant on oath and provide opportunity of cross examination of the witnesses so produced.

(3) The officer shall record in writing the statement of the witnesses on oath and in cross examination and take the documentary evidence on record.

(4) The officer shall, after the complainant's evidence is complete, provide an opportunity of defence to the accused person and the witnesses produced by the accused shall be cross examined after their statements on oath by the complainant and documentary evidence in defence shall be taken on record by the officer.

(5) The officer shall after hearing the parties and considering the evidence both oral and documentary, decide the complaint in accordance with the provisions of the Code.

Procedure of courts of inquiry

173. (1) The proceedings of a court of inquiry shall not be open to the public. Only such persons may attend the proceedings as are permitted by the court to do so.

(2) The evidence of all witnesses shall be taken on oath or affirmation.

(3) Evidence given by witnesses shall be recorded in narrative form unless the court considers that any questions and answers may be recorded as such.

(4) The court may take into consideration any documents even though they are not formally proved.

(5) The court may ask witnesses any question, in any form, that they consider necessary to elicit the truth and may take into consideration any evidence, whether the same is admissible under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872) or not.

(6) No counsel, or legal practitioner shall be permitted to appear before a court of inquiry.

(7) Provisions of section 89 shall apply for procuring the attendance of witnesses before the court of inquiry.

(8) Before giving an opinion against any person subject to the Act, the court will afford that person the opportunity to know all that has been stated against him, cross-examine any witnesses who have given evidence against him, and make a statement and call witnesses in his defence.

(9) The answers given by a witness to any question asked before the court shall not be admissible against such a witness on any charge at any subsequent occasion except a charge of giving false evidence before such court.

If the accused has pleaded guilty and does not challenge the evidence on record, the proceedings shall be closed for orders. If he pleads "Not guilty", he shall be required to file a written statement, and a list of such witnesses as he may wish to cite in his defence within such period, which shall in any case be not less than a fortnight, as the officer conducting enquiry may deem reasonable in the circumstances of the case. If he declines to file a written statement, he shall again be examined by the officer conducting the enquiry on the expiry of the period allowed.

(5)

If the accused refuses to cite any witnesses or to produce any evidence in his defence, the proceedings shall be closed for orders. If he produces any evidence the officer conducting the enquiry shall proceed to record the evidence. If the officer conducting the enquiry considers that the evidence of any witness or any document which the accused wants to produce in his defence is not material to the issues involved in the case, he may refuse to call such witness or to allow such document to be produced in evidence, but in all such cases he must briefly record his reasons for considering the evidence inadmissible. When all relevant evidence has been brought on record, the proceedings shall be closed for orders.

(6)

If the Commandant has himself held the enquiry, he shall record his findings and pass orders where he has power to do so. If the enquiry has been held by any officer other than the Commandant, the officer conducting the enquiry shall forward his report together with the proceedings, to the Commandant, who shall record his findings and pass orders, where he has power to do so.

44. (1) On receipt of a complaint of an offence committed under sub-sections (3), (5), (7), (8), (9), (10), (11) and (20) of section 86 and sub-section (7) of section 89, the complaint shall be enquired into by an officer not below the rank of Under Secretary to the Government of India, appointed by the Central Government for such purpose under sub- section (1) of section 85 (hereinafter referred to as the "enquiry officer").

(2) On receipt of the complaint, the enquiry officer shall call upon the person or persons through notice to be sent electronically, or by speed post and upload a copy of the same on the designated portal of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, to appear before him on a specified date together with all relevant documents and witnesses, if any, and shall inform the complainant of the date so specified.

(3) Where a party so desires, he may request in writing to the enquiry officer to issue notice in the enquiry only by post and also in cases where the enquiry officer feels that no electronic means of communication are available to the parties concerned, he may send such notice by speed post.

(4) In case the person to whom notice has been issued under sub-rule (2), the person or his representative fails to appear on the specified date, the enquiry officer may proceed to hear and determine the complaint ex-parte.

(5) In case the complainant fails to appear on the specified date without any information to the enquiry officer on two consecutive dates, the enquiry officer may dismiss the complaint:

Provided further that the enquiry officer shall at his discretion permit hearing the parties or any of the party, as the case may be, through video conferencing.

(7) Any person who intends to appear in the proceeding on behalf of the complainant shall present before the enquiry officer and submit a brief statement in writing explaining the reason for his appearance.

(8) The enquiry officer shall record an order on the statement referred to in sub-rule (7) permitting the person referred to in that sub-rule to appear in the proceeding on behalf of the complainant, and in the case of refusing such permission, the enquiry officer shall include reasons for the same and incorporate it in the record.

(9) The complaint or other documents relevant to the complaint may be presented in person to the enquiry officer at any time during hours fixed by the enquiry officer or may be sent to him electronically or by speed post and the opposite party shall have the right to reply to the complaint and such other documents.

(10) The enquiry officer shall endorse or cause to be endorsed on each document, the date of its presentation or receipt, as the case may be, and if the documents are submitted electronically, no such endorsement shall be necessary.

(11) The enquiry officer may refuse to entertain a complaint, if considers that the complaint is incomplete and may request the complainant to rectify the defects within the time specified for such purpose:

Provided that if the enquiry officer observes that it is not possible to rectify the defects in the complaint, he may at once return such complaint indicating the defects.

Procedure for enquiry into causes of accident or dangerous occurrence

.

211. (1) The enquiry under sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) of section 39 of the Act, as the case may be, shall be conducted by the authority referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-rule (1) of rule 210, in the following manner, namely:

(a)

the enquiry shall be commenced as early as it may be, and in any case, within fifteen days of the receipt of notice of accident or dangerous occurrence under rule 210;

(b)

the enquiry may be conducted by the authority referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-rule (1) of rule 210 himself or by an enquiry officer appointed by such authority;

(c)

the authority or enquiry officer, as the case may be, shall serve or cause to be served, notices in writing, informing the date, time and place of such enquiry to all persons entitled to appear in such enquiry and whose names and addresses are known to such authority or enquiry officer;

(d)

notwithstanding the provision of clause (b), for the purpose of notifying other persons who may in any way be concerned or be interested in such enquiry, the authority or enquiry officer, as the case may be, may publish notice of such enquiry in one or more local newspapers, informing the date, time and place of such enquiry.

(2) The person entitled to appear at the enquiry may include-

(a)

an inspector or any officer of the Central Government or the State Government or an undertaking or public body, concerned with the enforcement or compliance of safety provisions of the Act and the rules in the concerned establishment;

(b)

a trade union or a workers' association or an employers' association;

(c)

the worker involved in the accident or his legal heir or authorised representative;

(d)

the owner of the premises in which the accident took place;

(e)

any other person, at the discretion of the authority or the enquiring officer, as the case may be, who may be interested in or be concerned with the cause of an accident or may have knowledge about such cause or is likely to give material evidence or produce a relevant document in connection with such accident or dangerous occurrence.

(3) In case the entitled person referred to in sub-rule (2) is a body corporate, a company, or any other organisation, association, group of persons such group may be represented through an authorised representative including a counsel or a solicitor.

(4) Subject to the provisions of sub-rule (5), the enquiry shall be held in public.

(5) In cases where-

(a)

the Central Government is of the opinion that the matter of the enquiry or any part of it are of such nature that it would be against the interests of national security or any part of it are of such nature that it would be against the interests of national security to hold the enquiry in public and directs the said authority or the enquiry officer, as the case may be, to hold the enquiry in camera; or

(b)

on an application made by any party to the enquiry, the authority or the enquiry officer, as the case may be, referred to in sub-rule (1), if it or he is of the opinion that the holding of public enquiry will lead to disclosure of information relating to a trade secret, decides to hold the enquiry of such part of it in camera, such enquiry shall not be held in public.

(6) Information disclosed by any person during the course of hearing or evidence in the cases covered under sub-rule (5) shall not be disclosed to any person except for the purpose of the enquiry.

(7) The person entitled to appear under sub-rule (2), called for evidence or representing in an enquiry shall be entitled to make an opening statement, give evidence, request the enquiry officer to call for specified document or evidence, cross-examine other persons or to the extent and at the stage permitted by the authority or enquiry officer holding the enquiry.

(8) Any evidence in an enquiry may be admitted at the discretion of the authority or enquiry officer during the enquiry, who may, also direct that documents to be tendered in evidence may be inspected by any person entitled or permitted to appear at such enquiry and that facilities be afforded to such person to take or obtain copies thereof.

(9) The authority or the enquiry officer holding an enquiry may authorise any person, being an officer of the Central Government, to assist such authority or enquiry officer where necessary, for the purpose of conducting the enquiry, and the officer so authorised may enter the premises of the concerned establishment during working hours, inspect the records relevant to such enquiry, investigate and take such evidence as may be required to conduct such enquiry.

38. (1) The following acts shall constitute gross misconduct for the purposes of second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 68, namely:—

(a)

wilful destruction of employer's goods or property;

(b)

assaulting any superior or co-employee at the place of work;

(c)

criminal offence involving moral turpitude resulting in conviction in a court of law;

(d)

theft, fraud, or dishonesty in connection with the employer's business or property; and

(e)

wilful non-observance of safety measures or rules on the subject or wilful interference with safety devices or with firefighting equipment.

(2) (a) An appeal under sub-section (2) of section 68 shall be preferred to the competent authority in Form-XII;

(b) The appeal may be made in writing and either handed over personally or sent under a registered cover or electronically to the competent authority.

(c) When an appeal is received, the competent authority shall furnish a copy of the memorandum of appeal to the employer, call for his reply thereto and also ask him to produce documents connected with the issue of the appeal by fixing a date.

(d) The competent authority may ascertain further details, if necessary, from the employer as well as from the appellant, and he shall consider the facts presented to him, if any, and shall give his decision:

Provided that the Competent Authority shall dispose of the appeal within three months from the date of receipt of the appeal:

Provided further that the Competent Authority may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, extend the said period for a further period not exceeding three months.

(e) In case the employer fails to submit his reply or produce the required documents within the specified period, the competent authority may give his decision ex-parte.

52. (1) No order imposing any of the major penalties specified in regulation 51 shall be made except after an inquiry is held in accordance with this regulation.

(3) On receipt of the written statement of the employee, or if no such statement is received within the time specified, if it has been considered that there are grounds for inquiring into the truth of any imputation of misconduct or misbehavior against an employee, the Competent Authority may himself inquire into or appoint an inquiry officer to inquire into the truth thereof:

Provided that it may not be necessary to hold an inquiry in respect of the articles of charge admitted by the employee in his written statement but it shall be necessary to record its findings on each such charge.

(8) The employee shall appear before the Inquiry Officer at the time, place and date specified in the notice and the Inquiry Officer shall ask the employee whether he pleads guilty or as any defence to make and, if he pleads guilty to any of the articles of charge, the Inquiry Officer shall record the plea, sign the record and obtain the signature of the employee concerned thereon.

14. Stoppage of work and re-opening

(a)

Subject to the provisions of Chapter VA of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the employer may, at any time, in the event of underground trouble, fire, catastrophe, breakdown of machinery, stoppage of power supply, epidemic, civil commotion or any other cause beyond the control of the employer, stop any section or sections of the mine wholly or partially for any period or periods.

(b)

In the event of such stoppage during working hours, the workmen affected shall be notified by notice put up on the notice board in the department concerned and of the office as soon as practicable as to when work will be resumed and whether they are to remain or leave their place of work. The workmen will not ordinarily be required to remain for more than two hours after the commencement of the stoppage. Whenever workmen are laid off on account of failure of plant or a temporary curtailment of production or other causes they shall be paid compensation in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Where no such compensation is admissible, they shall be granted leave with or without wages, as the case may be, at the option of the workman concerned, leave with wages being granted to the extent of any leave due to them. When workmen are to be laid off for an indefinitely long period, their services may be terminated subject to the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. If normal work is resumed two weeks' notice hereof shall be given by the pasting of notices at or near the mine office and the workmen discharged earlier by the employer shall, if they present themselves for work, have preference for re-employment.

(c)

The employer may in the event of a strike affecting either wholly or partially any section of the mine close down either wholly or partially such section of the mine and any other section affected by such closure. The fact of such closure shall be notified by notices put up on notice board in the manager's office. Prior to resumption of work, the workmen concerned will be notified by a general notice indicating as to when work will be resumed. A copy of such notice shall be sent to the registered trade union or unions functioning in the establishment.

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 22 or 23 of the Act.

The reason here is the presumption that master is aware of what his servant is doing and that the servant is always deemed to act on behalf of and on the directions of the master. PROBLEMS WITH THE EXISTING JURISPRUDENCE

The most debatable topic since ages is whether a company can be made criminally liable. One might say imposition of fines is way of punishing a corporation, but that hardly resulted in any deterrence in the crimes by corporations. The main problem is the so called statutory inadequacy. And if one says lifting of corporate veil is a solution, there are again difficulties in identifying to whom exactly the evil intent belonged to. And in large companies it is impossible for the shareholders to control the management and directors, and therefore cannot be made liable.

The major problem is, though the definition of a 'person' includes a company, it is not possible to imprison a company being a juristic person. The courts find a dead end in cases where a corporation is charged under provisions providing for mandatory imprisonment as it cannot be imprisoned. The temporary solutions that courts have come up is to make companies liable for greater amounts fines. Also, there are problems in holding the agents liable, such as, identifying who controlling person was; do all the concerned staff have the same state of mind. In Moore v. Bresler Ltd.,34 an employee whose duty was to pay tax had not performed duty resulting in the guilt of the company, wherein the court stated that such act should be attributed to company irrespective of the fact that it was done to conceal his theft from the company. However the appellate court reverse the decision by holding that the sales were not made by them on behalf of the corporation but rather in fraud of the company itself. In India it is considered that knowledge is a pre-requisite before holding a company liable. This shows the attitude of Indian Criminal Law towards corporate crimes.

Another question which arises in the concept of CCL is the punishment. Can a corporation be imprisoned? The punishments which may be imposed to a corporation are imposing fine, forfeiture of its properties and cancelling of its license. In Northern Star Mining Corporation Ltd. case35, a company was prosecuted for manslaughter which was criticized to be inadequate. Again in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. J.B. Company,36 where the court held that company is not an exception to criminal law and that it could be tried for an offence for which imprisonment is the prescribed punishment, but will be fined.

CONCLUSION

Earlier, the concept of a separate legal entity of a company and of corporate veil created by statutory provisions, has been exploited to a great extent by individuals in order to evade personal liability, which lead to a well-established law worldwide, that a company can be made liable for criminal offences irrespective of looking into whether it had an evil intent or not. Though the laws in India are not developed as that of other countries for making a corporation completely liable, but it had to an extent developed the law through its judicial pronouncements. In spite of this, India has not gone beyond imposing of fines and forfeiture of property of a company, which mean that the laws in India are insufficient to deal with the present day cases.

Delhi Cloth General Mill v. Workmen, AIR 1967 SC 469

The case arose between the appellant and its two units Delhi Cloth and General Mills (DCM) and Swatantra Bharat Mills (SBM), rooted in the matter of bonus. As the matter of bonuses stayed unresolved, the workers turned violent in DCM. The management on the subsequent day declared a lock-out, as the situation did not improve. The workers in SBM unit, the very next day resorted to a stay-in-strike. In the report submitted by the conciliation officer, it was stated that an industrial dispute exited between the management and workmen. The appropriate government made a reference to the tribunal with issue 3 being whether the strike at the DCM and the lockout declared by the Management were justified and legal; and issue 4 being whether the, sit-down strike at the SBL was justified and legal. The tribunal considered it within its jurisdiction to adjudicate on whether there were strikes at the Mills at all and permitted the parties to adduce evidence in confirmation or denial of the existence of the strikes.

The Supreme Court held that the basis of issues 3 and 4 was that there were strikes at the two units and a lockout declared by the Management at one. Once the issues are framed, the tribunal's determination must be confined to adjudication of the specified issued and matters incidental thereto. The tribunal is neither permitted to examine facts challenging the issues set forth in the reference nor is it permitted to examine whether reference was wrongly worded. It is not free to enlarge the scope of the dispute referred to it but must confined its attention to the points specifically mentioned and anything which is incidental thereto. "Something incidental to a dispute means something happening as a result of or in connection with the dispute or associated with the dispute. The dispute is the fundamental thing while something incidental thereto is an adjunct to it. It cannot cut at the root of the main thin to which it is an adjunct."

Voluntary Arbitration

Arbitration is an alternate dispute resolution mechanism, which involves third party intervention. Although, arbitration has not been defined under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (ID Act), it can be understood as "a process of dispute resolution in which a neutral third party (arbitrator) renders a decision after a hearing at which both parties have an opportunity to be heard."31 The need for voluntary arbitration under ID Act are reiterated in the following observation of the Supreme Court:

"The voluntary arbitration is a part of infrastructure of dispensation of justice in the industrial adjudication. Voluntary arbitration appears to be the best method for settlement of industrial disputes. The disputes can be resolved speedily and in less than a year, typically in a few months. The Tribunal adjudication of reference under Section 10(1)often drags on for several years, thus defeating the very purpose of the industrial adjudication. Arbitration is also cheaper than litigation with less legal work and no motion practice. It has limited document discovery with quicker hearing and less formal than trials. The greatest advantage of arbitration is that there is no right of appeal, review or writ petition. Besides, it may, as well reduce company's litigation costs and its potential exposure to ruinous liability apart from redeeming the workmen from frustration."32

In the instant case, three members of the petitioner-Union were dismissed from service. The Management invoked section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, seeking approval for a penalty of dismissal. In the said proceeding, workmen took a stand that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper.

Evidence was led on the issue relating to the fairness of the domestic enquiry. The Labour Court, on appreciation of evidence led before it by both sides, held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper. Consequently, accorded approval for dismissal.

The Union later raised a dispute challenging the penalty of dismissal. Union contended that the domestic enquiry was not fair and proper. The Management urged that in a proceeding under section 33(2)(b), it had already been held that the domestic enquiry was fair and proper, and the said finding operates as res judicata and cannot be agitated again, in a proceeding challenging the penalty of dismissal of service.

The Labour Court accepted the Management's plea and declined to reconsider the said issue, holding that it operates as res judicata.

The High Court noted that the question as to whether domestic enquiry was fair and proper, if raised in an application under section 33(2)(b), and if finding on such an application is recorded after full-fledged enquiry, such finding is not just a prima facie finding on said question as to fairness and validity of domestic enquiry and it is a finding on adjudication which attains finality if not questioned, and cannot be re-agitated in subsequent proceedings between same parties.

Further, the High Court noted that a finding on an issue relating to the fairness of a domestic enquiry is adjudicatory and the said question cannot be revisited in an industrial dispute challenging a penalty.

The High Court held that the enquiry under section 33(2)(b) of the Act, as to whether the domestic enquiry was fair and proper (rendered after recording of evidence before the authority), is binding on parties to the proceedings. Since the authority has jurisdiction to adjudicate on the fairness of the domestic enquiry, such a finding cannot be re-agitated in a subsequent industrial dispute challenging the order of penalty, as it operates as res judicata between the same parties in subsequent proceedings.

Further, the authority under section 33(2)(b) cannot adjudicate on the merits of the findings in the domestic enquiry or on the penalty, as it lacks jurisdiction to do so. These issues can be adjudicated only in a subsequent industrial dispute, if raised.

Court in Crompton Greaves Ltd. v. Workmen (AIR 1978 SC 1489) observed that a strike is a legal weapon available to workers. However, its justification depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The Court clarified that even an illegal strike may be justified in rare situations, while a legal strike may still be unjustified if the conduct of workers is unreasonable.

3.1-2. Whether a lockout is the same as the closure of operations? The Supreme Court in Management of Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Workers & Staff Employed Under it (AIR 1963 SC 569) clarified that a lockout is not the same as a closure. A lockout refers to the temporary closing of the place of employment, the suspension of work, or the employer's refusal to employ workers during an industrial dispute. A closure, on the other hand, refers to the permanent shutdown of business operations. Unlike a lockout, a closure signifies the end of business itself, not just the temporary suspension of operations.

Further, in Management of Kairbetta Estate v. Rajamanickam (AIR 1960 SC 893), the Supreme Court elaborated on the distinction between a lock-out and a lay-off. The Court held that a layoff arises when ongoing operations exist but workers cannot be given work due to reasons beyond the employer's control, while a lockout involves a temporary suspension of operations by the employer. In this case, a justified lockout in response to workers' violence cannot be treated as a layoff, and thus, the workers were not entitled to layoff compensation.

3.2 Prohibition on Strikes and Lockouts:

The provisions relating to the prohibition on strikes and lockouts are as follows:

3.2-1 Prohibition on Strikes

No person employed in an industrial establishment must go on strike, in breach of contract, in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving the employer a notice of strike within 60 days before striking or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of strike specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.2-2 Prohibition on Lockouts

No employer of an industrial establishment must lock out any of his workers in any of the following circumstances:

(a)

Without giving a notice of lock-out within 60 days before locking out or

(b)

Within 14 days of giving such notice or

(c)

Before the expiry of the date of lock-out specified in such notice or

(d)

During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(e)

During the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion of such proceedings, or

(f)

During the pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator and 60 days after the conclusion of such proceedings or

(g)

During any period in which a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by such settlement or award.

3.3 Exemption from notice requirement in case of existing strike or lockout:

The notice of strike or lockout must not be necessary where a strike or lockout is already in existence. However, the employer must send intimation of such lock-out or strike on the day on which it is declared to such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government, either generally or for a particular area or for a particular class of services.

3.4 Reporting Requirements for Strikes and Lockout Notices:

If on any day, an employer receives from any person employed by him, any notice or gives to any person employed by him, any notice of strike or lock-out, he must report it within 5 days to the appropriate Government or to such authority as the Government may prescribe and to the conciliation officer, specifying the number of notices received or issued on that day.

3.5 Illegality of Strikes and Lockouts:

A strike or lock-out must be considered illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 62 or continued in violation of an order made under Section 42(7) of the Code.

3.5-1. When continuation of a strike or lock-out is not deemed illegal

If a strike or lock-out relating to an industrial dispute has already commenced and is in existence at the time an application is filed before the Tribunal or when the dispute is referred to an arbitrator or the National Industrial Tribunal, its continuance shall not be deemed illegal. The only condition is that the strike or lock-out was legal when it began and has not been prohibited.

3.5-2. Legality of strikes or lock-outs declared in consequence of illegality

A lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike or a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out must not be considered illegal.

Sometimes it happens that law’s delays become intolerable and justice becomes sour. In the trial of offences under this law, there are certain stages as enumerated hereinabove.

NEED TO DO AWAY WITH EMPTY FORMALITIES

2. Now for curtailing delays in the trial, some short cuts should be evolved and some empty formalities should be eliminated. As we all know in matters of proceedings under the Negotiable Instruments Act, the delay has been defeating the very purpose of enacting this law. Unfortunately on account of delays sanctity, integrity and credibility of issuance of cheques in commercial transaction is getting eroded to a large extent. The pendency of large number of complaints has promoted the judiciary to get aware of this malaise and in this sequence, the Mumbai High Court in the case of KSL & Industries Ltd. v. Mannalal Khandelwal [2005] Cr. LJ 1201 has come out with certain suggestions for cutting down the delays in trial of cases under this Act. The Court felt that it had become imperative for it to take all the necessary steps that are necessary for disposal of complaints expeditiously so that unscrupulous people do not take undue advantage of the pendency of the complaint for a long time. For suggesting suitable measures in this regard, the Court first visualized the various stages through which the complaint passes during trial.

2.1 QUICK AND SIMPLIFIED PROCEDURE - This elaborate procedure causes enormous delay in disposal of the cases as observed by Justice Dalvir Bhandari, (Justice as he then was) in the Delhi High Court. In United Ink and Varnish Co. Ltd. v. State [2000] 6 Comp. LJ 444, he held that the manner in which these complaints are dealt with by trial courts, it could take 8 to 10 years before the cases are finally adjudicated. The delays are attributable to several reasons such as poor infrastructure facilities of trial Court, shortage of judicial officers, over burdening of cases, etc. But this should not mean that the complaints should linger on for years together. It has therefore, been suggested that to cut down delay, the complainant should be examined positively within 3 months and then the examination of other witnesses could be done by means of an affidavit and the witnesses could be cross-examined at the request of the accused and most importantly, the accused should be summoned quickly through all modes of serving the summons, viz., registered AD, speed post, Courts process server and then finally, it should be ensured that the complaints are invariably disposed of within 6 months after the complainant has been examined. Then the Registrar General of every High Court should monitor that these directions are carried out and the concerned High Court must seek a quarterly report from the subordinate Courts in regard to cases under this Act.

2.2 EFFECTIVE SERVICE OF SUMMONS - It is submitted that a significant part of the delay in the commencement of trial of such complaints in Indian Magisterial Courts can be attributed to the delays usually experienced in following and completing of the very preliminary procedure of service of summons upon the accused persons. In cases of bounced cheques, this delay could be for several months even for years together. If we could secure the service of summons on accused much of the delays could be eliminated in this respect. While referring to sections 62 to 65 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the mandates of section 65 read as here-under—

Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided - "If service cannot, by the exercise of due diligence, be effected as provided in section 62, 63 or 64, the serving officer shall affix one of the duplicates of the summons to some conspicuous part of the house or homestead in which the person summoned ordinarily resides; and thereupon the Court, after making such enquiries as it thinks fit, may either declare that the summons has been duly served or order fresh service in such manner as it considers proper".

The Court should, therefore, direct the serving officer that if the service cannot be effected as provided under sections 62 to 64, then the service should be effected under section 65 of the Code without any specific order in this regard. If that is done, things would become very easy and the top most situation of indefensible and unconscionable judicial delays in effecting service upon the accused would be eliminated and this would help commencement of trial of bounced cheque cases within a reasonable period after process have been served. It is also submitted that this simple and perfectly lawful innovation will considerably cut down the current delay in trial of cases under the Negotiable Instruments Act.

The provisions of section 65 of Cr. P.C. makes it mandatory and obligatory on the part of serving officer to effect service by pasting summons at the place where accused ordinarily resided.

CONCLUSION

3. The stringent deterrents as spelled out in the Act would be eaten away by the delays in the trial of cases under the Act and, therefore, it is now very essential that we should now put up all our energy in exploring ways and means of securing speedy trial of the offenders of bounced cheques. This is in tune with our fast track culture in dealing with pending cases.

"Sententia Legis" is a very well known Rule of interpretation of statue which says that an essence of the law lies in the spirit, not in its letter, but letters are the only way in which intentions are expressed. The words are external manifestation of intention that it involves. When there is possibility of one or more interpretation of statute, court has to adopt that interpretation which reflects the 'true intention of legislature'.

Hon'ble Supreme Court also in a landmark judgment Kailash v.Nanhku[2005] 4 SCC 480 held that:

"All the rules of procedure are the handmaid of justice. The language employed by the draftsman of processual law may be liberal or stringent, but the fact remains that the object of prescribing procedure is to advance the cause of justice. In an adversarial system, no party should ordinarily be denied the opportunity of participating in the process of justice dispensation. Unless compelled by express and specific language of the statute, the provisions of CPC or any other procedural enactment ought not to be construed in a manner which would leave the court helpless to meet extraordinary situations in the ends of justice."

So, we can say that legislature included note in Form 5 with an intention to allow workers to file suit individually as well as jointly. Therefore, Section 9 of the IBC can be interpreted in a way so that true intention of the legislature must be satisfied. Hence, under Section 9 of IBC joint suit by the registered Trade Union on behalf of workers is permissible.

Preponderance of Probability 6. In a case of clandestine activity involving suppression of production and clandestine removal it is not expected that such evasion has to be established by the Department in a mathematical precision. After all a person indulging in clandestine activity takes sufficient precautions to hide/destroy the evidence. Some evidence may be left in spite of the best care taken by the persons involved in such clandestine activity. In such a situation, the entire facts and circumstances of the case have to be looked into and a decision has to be arrived at on the yardstick of 'preponderance of probability' and not on the yardstick of 'beyond reasonable doubt', as the decision is being rendered in quasi-judicial proceedings.

CCE 2001 (130) ELT 271 (Tri. - Kol) the notebook entries of production and removal of products recovered from a person whose name was appearing in the list of workers in statutory records could not be of any relevance to establish the charge of clandestine manufacture and removal. Such a charge could not be sustained on presumption that the persons entrusted with such job were not usually shown as employees. The entries in private notebook of record of production at the most may raise a doubt but cannot be a proof of the charge in the absence of corroborative evidence, like installed capacity of factory, raw material utilization, labour employed, power consumed, goods actually manufactured and packed.

Further, the manufacturer of such goods also did not stand established. The allegations of clandestine removal were required to be substantiated by positive and tangible evidences and could not be upheld on the mere assumptions and presumptions. The confirmation of demand on the basis of photo copies provided by the informer could not be upheld in the absence of any evidence.

It has been the consistent stand of quasi-judicial and judicial appellate forums that for establishing the facts of clandestine removal there need to be sufficient evidence on record leading to conclusive proof of production of goods, their removal from the factory by any mode of transportation and clandestine clearance to the buyers. Mere doubts, howsoever strong, cannot take the place of evidence required to be produced by the revenue. The onus to establish such clandestine activities, resulting in confirmation of demand is placed heavily on the Revenue and is required to be discharged by production of sufficient evidence.

1. Introduction

Industrial peace and harmony are essential to any nation's economic and social progress. However, differences between employers and employees are inevitable in an industrial setup, often leading to disputes over wages, working conditions, employment security or management decisions. When such disputes escalate without resolution, they may culminate in strikes or lockouts.

Both strikes and lockouts are integral components of the collective bargaining process, serving as pressure tools in industrial negotiations. While a strike reflects the workers' expression of protest or demand, a lockout symbolises the employers' countermeasure to ensure operational discipline.

In India, the right to strike is not a fundamental right, but a statutory right, subject to legal restrictions under labour legislation. Similarly, lockouts are lawful only when they are conducted in compliance with specific legal procedures. Historically, these aspects were governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which laid the foundation for industrial relations in post-independence India.

However, with the evolution and diversification of industrial activities, the need for a more unified, integrated and simplified legal structure has become evident. This led to the enactment of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, one of four labour codes introduced by the Government of India to consolidate, modernise and rationalise existing labour laws.

2. Legal Framework under Industrial Relations Code, 2020

The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, represents a major reform in India's labour law landscape. It consolidates and replaces three key statutes:

(a)

The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947: This Act was intended to provide workers with a mechanism that would provide relief against layoffs, downsizing and wrongful termination that is against the letter of the law. It also sought to promote healthy labour relations by minimizing the scope for illegal strikes and lockouts and penalizing unfair labour practices.

(b)

The Trade Unions Act, 1926: This Act aimed to provide workers with better working conditions, better wages, protection against abusive employment, the right to form an association and collective negotiation. It facilitated the organisation of the workers' union and allowed greater participation of the workforce in the management of the establishment.

(c)

Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946: This Act regulates the conditions of employment, grievances, misconduct, etc. of the workers employed in the industry.

It is to be noted that the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, was passed by Parliament and received the President's assent on September 28, 2020. The Code has now come into force with effect from November 21, 2025, following the issuance of the notification by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. Accordingly, the provisions of the Code have become operational from this date, replacing the earlier labour laws that were previously in effect.

3. Key provisions relating to Strikes and Lockouts under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020

The key provisions relating to strikes and lockouts are detailed under Sections 62 to 67 of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

3.1 Definitions: Strikes and lockouts are defined as below:

(a)

'Strike' [Section 2(zk)] - means a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal, or a refusal, under a common understanding, of any number of persons who are or have been so employed to continue to work or to accept employment and includes the concerted casual leave on a given day by 50% or more workers employed in an industry.

(b)

'Lockout' [Section 2(u)] – refers to the temporary closing of a place of employment, or the suspension of work, or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him.

3.1-1. Do workers have a fundamental right to strike in India?

The Supreme Court in T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu and others [2003] taxmann.com 3831 (SC)held that the right to strike is not a fundamental right. In fact, there is no legal/statutory right to go on strike. Apart from statutory rights, Government employees cannot claim that they can take the society at ransom by going on strike. Further, there is a prohibition on going on strike under the Tamil Nadu Government Servants Conduct Rules, 1973.

Additionally, the Supreme Court in Crompton Greaves Ltd. v. Workmen (AIR 1978 SC 1489) observed that a strike is a legal weapon available to workers. However, its justification depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The Court clarified that even an illegal strike may be justified in rare situations, while a legal strike may still be unjustified if the conduct of workers is unreasonable.

Following loopholes are noteworthy :—

(i) Rule 12CC of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 and rule 12AA of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 are ultra vires the Central Excise Act : Section 37 of the Central Excise Act empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry into effect the purposes of the Act but the rules are clearly beyond the power vested in the Central Government. Section 37(2) lays down the purposes for which rules could be made. Section 37(3), 37(4) and 37(5) provide for the penalties that could be provided for in the rules. However, the above provisions do not empower the Central Government to impose penalties as specified in Notification No. 32 of 2006, which provides for restrictions on utilization of CENVAT credit.

In V.K. Ashokan v. Asstt. Excise Commnr.11, it was held that the power to frame rules and the power to impose terms and conditions thereof are subject to the provisions of the parent Act. They must conform to the legislative policy. The Supreme Court further laid down that rules framed or other terms and conditions imposed under an Act should not be contrary to the other provisions of the Act and must not be framed in contravention of the constitutional or statutory scheme.

(ii) The impugned notifications are violative of article 14 of the Constitution of India : The impugned notifications constitute a direct attack on the right to equality enshrined in article 14 as it confers unbridled power12 on the Member (Central Excise), an officer authorized by the Board, to pass order restricting utilization of the validly earned CENVAT credit, for 6 months, in utter violation of principles of natural justice13

(ii)(A) Conferment of unbridled power on the Member (Central Excise) : Under clause 4(3) of Notification No. 32 of 2006, the Member is not required to give any hearing to the accused before passing an order specifying the type of facilities to be withdrawn and restrictions to be imposed, which have dire civil consequences14 .

In State of Orissa v. Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei15, it was held that when by reason of an action on the part of a statutory authority, civil or evil consequences ensue, principles of natural justice are required to be followed. In such an event, although no express provision is laid down in this behalf, compliance of principles of natural justice would be implicit. In case of denial of principles of natural justice in a particular statute, the same may also be held ultra vires article 14.

Further, it is a cardinal rule of jurisprudence that whosoever has heard the case, should adjudicate over it16. In the instant case, the Member who passes the order will not hear the accused, as the CC, whose role is limited merely to forwarding the proposal to the Member is the authority designated to hear the accused. Thus, it is based on such data and records, as provided by the CC, that the Member is expected to pass the orders. Therefore, the hearing proceedings are unusual and are clearly violative of principles of natural justice.

Also, under Notification No. 32 of 2006, there is no requirement for disclosure of the documents on the basis of which the authorities purport to take the stipulated actions.

In Kothari Filaments v. Commissioner of Customs (Port)17, the Apex Court has held that a person charged with mis-declaration is entitled to know the ground on the basis of which he would be penalized. He may or may not have an answer to the charges. But there cannot be any doubt whatsoever that in law he is entitled to a proper hearing which necessarily includes supply of the documents on the basis of which he is sought to be penalised. This is based on the simple logic that only on knowing the contents of a document, one could be expected to furnish an effective reply.

The provisions of rules 12CC and 12AA apply in order to prevent evasion of, and default in payment of, central excise duty but there is no requirement of the disclosure of documents by the authorities to show that there has been evasion of duty. This provision is, therefore, unique in nature and is entirely against the notion of rule of law, as embeded in Indian legal system.

Further, establishment of a prima facie case also requires giving opportunity of hearing and evidence18. In the instant case, as no hearing would be given by adjudicating authority and no evidences would be relied upon by the Member, under law even a prima facie case would not be made out.

In the light of the above assertions, it appears that the delegation of power is unrestrained and, hence, violative of article 14.

ESOS/ESOP benefits are granted these days by employers to pass on the profits of the company to employees at the cost of certain amount of share value which is lesser than its intrinsic net-worth or market value. The expenditure/loss incurred by the company is treated by the department as capital in nature. The author of this article examines the nature of ESOS/ESOP in the hands of an employee and equates it with production incentives/bonus/staff welfare expenditure. He cites case law wherein similar expenditure has been held to be allowable. The author concludes that ESOS/ESOP benefit provided by a company to its employees as per the approved guidelines framed by SEBI is well in accordance with the law and, accordingly, a company is entitled to claim the deferred-employees ESOS/ESOP compensation expenditure as business expenditure incurred by it wholly and exclusively for the purpose of its business - EDITOR

The background

1. It has been the struggle by every labour/trade union against the management of industry or Governments that the work force should be entitled to participate in the management as well profits of an industry. In fact, the revolution in the 17th century in England as well as in various countries was the benchmark for such struggle and this struggle has been continued by various trade unions/labour unions to avail them a share in not only management of industries but as well as in the profits of such units. The rationale behind their struggle is well recognized even in the law of economics, that Labour is one of the factors of production, the remaining being Land, Capital and Organisation.

In this pursuit, there has been an assertion from various segments of the Government as well as the judiciary that such right of participation has to be recognized. It is pertinent to note here that in a classic case decided by the Supreme Court in National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan [1983] 53 Comp. Cas 184, it was held that workers are entitled to be heard before a company is directed to be wound up. In this case, the question arose as to whether when the Court was deciding a petition to wind-up the company, the workmen employed by the company had the right to be heard by the Court, not as creditors of the company for dues outstanding but because they were likely to be deprived of the means of livelihood if the company was wound up. By a majority of 3 to 2, the Court (at p. 200 et. seq.) held that since the right to apply for winding up is a creature of statute and is available only to those mentioned in the statute, the workers cannot prefer a winding up petition against the company. However, it does not follow as a necessary consequence that the workers have no right to appear and be heard in support or opposition to winding up petition. The Court held that there was nothing in the Companies Act, 1956, expressly prohibiting workers from being heard though as interveners and not as parties. The Court further held that after the winding up order was made, the workers could appeal against it, but once the order became final, the workers could not participate in any further proceedings in the course of winding up. This case was followed in Katha Factory Mazdoor Sangh v. Laxmi Industrial & Trading Co. (P.) Ltd. [1988] 2 Comp. LJ 67 (All.) See also Narendra Glass Works (P.) Ltd. v. M.P. Beer Products (P.) Ltd. [1989] 65 Comp. Cas. 396 (MP). Thereafter, in several cases of either reconstruction or revival or closure of industrial undertakings, giving an opportunity of being heard to such of those labour unions has been recognized as one of the fundamental principles in administration, reconstruction or closure of a company under company law.

Towards this end, the Government of India, having recognized the importance of participation of work force in management of an industry, evolved a scheme through the Securities Exchange Board of India, Ministry of Finance which is popularly known as Securities Exchange Board of India (Employees Stock Option Scheme and Employees stock Purchase Scheme) Guidelines, 1999.

The section also provides that, where a strike in pursuance of an industrial dispute has already started and is in existence at the time of filing of the application relating to such industrial dispute in the Tribunal or of its reference to an arbitrator or a National Industrial Tribunal, the continuance of such strike or lock-out shall not be considered to be illegal, if the same was not at its commencement in contravention of the provisions of the Code or its continuance was not prohibited under sub-section (7) of Section 42. Lastly, it provided that a strike in consequence of an illegal lock-out shall not be deemed to be illegal.

3.3. Comparison Between Industrial Disputes Act and Industrial Relations Code

On a comparison between the two statutes, it can be observed that there has not been any substantial change in the provisions of Strike and the new sections have to a great extent been enacted mutatis mutandis in the new Code. The only notable changes that can be observed are firstly, in the definition of strike, as hereafter even a concerted casual leave of fifty percent or more workers on a single day has been brought under the ambit of strike and secondly, in the time period of advance notice that must be given by the workers to the employers, has been increased from six weeks to 60 days. These two changes, do not in any manner appear to be conducive to the right to strike of workers, as it makes the definition of strike, clearer, categorical and restrictive in its words and also prevents them from making a prompter demonstration of their demands, respectively. Thus, the tone of these changes manifest that the legislature has, like the judiciary taken a more holistic view of the situation and the possible socio-economic ramifications of a strike. In the case of T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt. of T.N.6 the Court acknowledged that even if there was injustice to some extent, as it must have been presumed by such persons going on strike, in any democratic welfare state it was necessary that the aggrieved resorted to the machinery provided under the respective statute for the redressal of their grievances. Use of strike as a means, resulted in chaos and total misadministration, it affected the society as a whole and when it involved a great mass of people, it brought the entire system to a complete halt.

Thus, agreeing, that the negatives of strike were on a heavier side than its positives, the Code has sought to increase the role of peaceful dispute resolution mechanisms like arbitration, mediation and conciliation and has thus shown more keenness towards the achievement of industrial and social peace and has sought to provide the parties with some more time so as to give them as well as their employees, a better chance to come on the same page.

4. Conclusion

The new IR Code has not made any significant change in the provisions for strike, which can attract a lot of eyes towards it, however there are a few changes which could be kept in mind, to understand the approach of the legislature towards it. The Code has included within the definition of strike, even the concerted casual leaves of more than fifty percent of the workers on any given particular day and has also increased the period of giving advance notice from six weeks to 60 days, thereby clearly manifesting the intention of the legislature, of precluding the instances of strike. The IR Code appears to have critically taken into consideration the negative impact of strikes on the overall social and economic fabric of the country and in view of the current state of economy of the Country, where there are high levels of unemployment and there is a great want of Investment by foreign and domestic players, the legislature could not bring any favourable change in law, for the workers and has, though not excessively, but evidently diluted the provisions relating to right to strike in the Code in comparison to the provisions contained in the ID Act.

5.2 Mechanism for Resolution of Industrial Disputes ( Rule 23)

The mechanism for the resolution of Industrial Disputes is as follows –

5.2-1 Conduct of Conciliation Proceedings The Rules prescribe the procedure for conciliation proceedings, including the submission of statements, the filing of affidavits and evidence, the reporting of outcomes, and the recording of settlements. The employer's and workers' representatives are required to submit their respective statements at the first meeting of the conciliation proceedings. All evidence, except documentary evidence, and all applications, replies, or rejoinders must be filed in the form of affidavits.

5.2-2 Initiation of Conciliation Proceedings

Upon receipt of a notice of strike13 or lock-out14, an application relating to an existing industrial dispute, or information regarding the apprehension of an industrial dispute, the conciliation officer is required to enter the details on the designated portal and initiate the prescribed action.

5.2-3 Powers and Functions of Conciliation Officer

The conciliation officer may take such action as may be required, including holding conciliation proceedings, examining the application, transferring matters falling within the jurisdiction of the State Government, or issuing notices to the concerned parties, as the case may be.

5.2-4 Inquiry and Facilitation of Settlement

The conciliation officer must promptly ascertain the facts and circumstances of the dispute, inquire into all matters affecting its merits and settlement, and take such steps as are considered necessary to facilitate a fair and amicable resolution between the parties.

5.2-5 Reporting where no settlement is reached

Where no settlement is reached, the conciliation officer must, within seven days of the conclusion of the proceedings, upload a report on the designated portal of the Ministry of Labour and Employment and forward a copy to the parties concerned and the Central Government.

5.2-6 Reporting of Settlement to Central Government

Where a settlement is reached, the conciliation officer must upload the report and the memorandum of settlement to the designated portal and submit them to the Central Government or its authorised officer.

6. Provisions Governing Strikes and Lock-outs

Rules 25 and 26 specify provisions relating to strikes and lock-outs.

6.1 Notice of Strike

The rules provide that the notice of a strike must be given to the employer of an industrial establishment in Form-XI, which must be duly signed by the Secretary of the concerned registered trade union or, where there is no registered trade union, by five elected representatives of the workers.

6.2 Intimation of notice of Strike by Employer

Where an employer of an industrial establishment receives any notice of strike from any person employed, then the employer shall, within five days from the date of receiving such notice, inform the same electronically to the concerned conciliation officer and Chief Labour Commissioner (Central).

6.3 Notice of Lock-out by Employer

The employer of an industrial establishment must give notice of lock-out in Form-XII to the Secretary of every registered trade union by registered post, speed post, or electronically. The notice must be clearly visible by the employer on the notice board or an electronic board at the main entrance to the industrial establishment.

6.4 Intimation of Lock-out Notice by Employer

Also, if the employer gives any person employed by him a notice of lock-out, he must, within five days from the date of such notice, electronically inform the concerned conciliation officer and the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central).

7. Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure ( Rule 27-36)

The provisions relating to lay-offs, retrenchment and closure are as follows:

7.1 General Provisions for Lay-offs, Retrenchment and Closure

Chapter IX of the Industrial Relations Code governs provisions relating to lay-offs15, retrenchment16 and closure17. The provisions of this chapter shall apply to industrial establishments employing fifty or more workers, or industrial establishments that are not of seasonal character.

7.1-1 Intimation of Notice of Retrenchment

The employer of the industrial establishment must serve prior notice of retrenchment in Form-XIII to the Central Government and to the concerned Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) via email or through speed post.

7.1-1 Timeline for serving notice of retrenchment

The notice of retrenchment must be served in the following manner:

(a)

When prior notice is given to the worker: The notice of retrenchment must be served within three days from the date of serving the notice.

(b)

Where wages are paid in lieu of notice: Where no prior notice is given to the worker, and he is paid one month of wages, the notice of retrenchment must be sent within three days from the date of payment of such wages.

Minimum Advance Notice Requirement: The notice of retrenchment must be sent to the Central Government and a copy to the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) at least one month before such date.

Reliance on the Supreme Court decision

3. The Circular draws reference to the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The Apex Court observed that "As is well known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a stay or suspension of the Order appealed against". It should be noted that this decision of the Apex Court was somewhat in a different context and was issued when the service tax was not even in force. In fact, the decision was passed by the Apex Court in favour of the assessee.

The appeal before the Apex Court was preferred by the Collector of Customs against the judgment of the Delhi Tribunal. The assessee, Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., imported machinery and classified as a 'Bevel Gear Generator'. The Customs authorities raised an objection and classified the machinery as 'Bevel Gear Planer', thereby confiscating the machinery.

The assessee was given an option to pay a redemption fine of Rs. 70,000/- and penalty of Rs. 10,000/- and clear the goods. Assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The appeal was allowed by the Tribunal which agreed with the classification claimed by the assessee. The counsel for the assessee requested that the customs authorities may be directed to issue a detention certificate for the entire period during which the goods were detained till the date of issuance of the detention certificate.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee by virtue of which the respondent was entitled to clear the machinery without payment of any duty. But the respondent required a detention certificate to clear the machinery. Evidently, in view of this problem, the Apex Court made the following interim order:

"Having heard Ld. Counsel for the Collector of Customs, Bombay and M/s. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., we direct that the application made by the latter for a detention certificate should not be rejected on the ground that the Appeal is pending in this Court against the Order of the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi."

However,when the assessee applied for issuance of a detention certificate, no such certificate was issued. The assessee submitted that the action of the authorities is relatable to and influenced by the public notice issued by the Collector of Customs, Bombay on July 25, 1985. So far as the detention certificate for a period exceeding six months is concerned, it can be issued only with the approval of and under the signature of the Collector. Para 4 of the public notice deals with issue of detention certificates to the parties succeeding in appeals and read as follows:

"Detention Certificate, as a rule, will be issued by the concerned competent Customs Authority to the Appellants succeeding in Appeals on receipt of the copies of such Orders which the latter making formal application for issue of Detention Certificates. However, in cases where the Customs House decides to go in second Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, the issue of Detention Certificate will be considered only after such second appeal is finally disposed of in favour of the parties."

The Apex Court held as follows:

"6. According to the above mentioned para 4, the goods will not be released even where the party succeeds in cases where the Customs Authorities decide to go in Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court. They will consider the issuance of such certificate only after the decision of the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. The Counsel for the assessee characterised the direction as arbitrary and contrary to law. We see the force in his submission. If the authorities are of the opinion that the goods ought not to be released pending the Appeal, the straight forward course for them is to obtain an Order of Stay or other appropriate direction from the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. Without obtaining such an Order they cannot refuse to implement the Order under Appeal. As is well-known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a Stay or suspension of the Order appealed against. Moreover, such detention is likely to create several complications relating to the demurrage charges besides the possible deterioration of the machinery and goods. We hope and trust that the Collector of Custom Bombay shall appropriately revise the said public notice in the light of the observations made herein. If he does not do so, there is a likelihood of the Customs Authorities being themselves made liable for demurrage charges in appropriate cases.

5.1 Maintenance of Registers, Records and Annual Returns

Rule 53 prescribes the requirements for maintaining registers, records, and returns under the Code on Social Security, 2020.
